title: Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser Theorem
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: In a nearly integrable Hamiltonian system, most invariant tori with sufficiently irrational frequencies survive small perturbations and form a Cantor set of positive measure.
latex: H(I,\theta)=h(I)+\varepsilon f(I,\theta) \Rightarrow \text{Cantor family of invariant tori}
short: Order survives small perturbations, but not everywhere.
long: Order survives small perturbations, but not everywhere. The surviving tori have Diophantine frequency vectors; resonant tori generally break.
proof: Iterate Newton-like coordinate transformations satisfying Diophantine nonresonance conditions, with measure estimates on the removed resonant sets.
consequence: It explains long-term stability in nearly integrable mechanical systems.

title: Sharkovsky Ordering of Periodic Points
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For a continuous map of an interval, existence of a period-m point forces periods that follow m in the Sharkovsky ordering; period three comes first and forces all periods.
short: One period forces a whole cascade of others in a surprising order.
long: One period forces a whole cascade of others in a surprising order. The ordering is a total order on the positive integers with 3 at the head and 1 at the tail.
proof: Analyse the interval images of a period-m orbit and construct periodic points via the intermediate value theorem.
consequence: It gives a sharp existence theory for periodic points of one-dimensional maps.

title: Euler Reflection Formula for the Gamma Function
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: For every complex z that is not an integer, the Gamma function satisfies a product identity with the sine function.
short: Gamma values at complementary arguments multiply to a trigonometric reciprocal.
long: Gamma values at complementary arguments multiply to a trigonometric reciprocal. It gives Gamma(1/2) = sqrt(pi) and controls the poles at nonpositive integers.
proof: Combine the Weierstrass product for Gamma with the Euler product for sine.
consequence: It evaluates many definite integrals and fixes analytic continuation normalisations.

title: Beta–Gamma Integral Identity
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The beta integral equals a quotient of Gamma functions whenever the real parts of its parameters are positive.
short: A finite-interval integral is a ratio of Gamma functions.
long: A finite-interval integral is a ratio of Gamma functions. The same identity holds for the integral over the positive real line after the substitution t = u/(1+u).
proof: Write Gamma(a)Gamma(b) as a double integral over the positive quadrant and change variables to separate the beta integral.
consequence: It unifies probability normalising constants with special-function algebra.

title: Legendre Duplication Formula
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Gamma function satisfies a doubling relation linking Gamma(z), Gamma(z+1/2), and Gamma(2z).
short: Halving the argument introduces a power of two and sqrt(pi).
long: Halving the argument introduces a power of two and sqrt(pi). It is the case p=2 of the Gauss multiplication theorem.
proof: Apply the beta integral with a=b=z and the substitution t=(1+u)/2.
consequence: It simplifies normalisations of beta and chi-square distributions.

title: Stirling's Asymptotic Formula for n!
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Factorials grow like sqrt(2 pi n)(n/e)^n, with a logarithmic expansion whose leading correction is of order 1/n.
short: Laplace's method turns the integral for n! into elementary asymptotics.
long: Laplace's method turns the integral for n! into elementary asymptotics. The full Stirling series is divergent but optimally truncatable.
proof: Apply Laplace's method to Gamma(n+1) = integral of x^n exp(-x) over x positive.
consequence: It is indispensable in combinatorics, statistics, and statistical mechanics.

title: Legendre Polynomial Orthogonality
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Legendre polynomials are orthogonal on the interval from minus one to one with a normalisation depending on the degree.
short: Different angular momenta give independent modes.
long: Different angular momenta give independent modes. They arise as eigenfunctions of a singular Sturm–Liouville problem with weight one.
proof: Use Rodrigues' formula and integrate by parts n times; boundary terms vanish because (x^2-1)^n has n-fold zeros at the endpoints.
consequence: It enables spectral expansion of functions on the sphere with axial symmetry.

title: Three-Term Recurrence for Orthogonal Polynomials
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Monic orthogonal polynomials for a positive measure satisfy a three-term recurrence whose subdiagonal coefficients are positive.
short: Orthogonality forces locality in the polynomial basis.
long: Orthogonality forces locality in the polynomial basis. The coefficients encode the moments of the underlying measure.
proof: Expand xP_n in the orthogonal basis; orthogonality kills all but three terms, and positivity of squared norms gives b_n>0.
consequence: It underlies stable evaluation and the Lanczos algorithm.

title: Christoffel–Darboux Identity
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The reproducing kernel for orthogonal polynomials has a closed two-term form involving the last two polynomials and the ratio of leading coefficients.
short: A long sum collapses to a short determinantal formula.
long: A long sum collapses to a short determinantal formula. Here k_n denotes the leading coefficient of the n-th orthonormal polynomial.
proof: Apply the three-term recurrence at x and y, multiply crosswise, subtract, and telescope the sum.
consequence: It gives reproducing kernels, Christoffel numbers, and sharp kernel bounds.

title: Jacobi Elliptic Functions and Doubly Periodic Meromorphy
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Jacobi elliptic functions are doubly periodic meromorphic functions generalising sine and cosine, and the function sn satisfies a first-order algebraic differential equation.
short: Elliptic functions invert elliptic integrals.
long: Elliptic functions invert elliptic integrals. The modulus k controls the ratio of the two periods; limiting cases give ordinary trigonometric or hyperbolic functions.
proof: Invert the integral from zero to phi of dtheta/sqrt(1-k^2 sin^2 theta) and differentiate.
consequence: They parametrise pendulum motion and nonlinear wave profiles.

title: Euler–Maclaurin Summation Formula
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A finite sum differs from the corresponding integral by endpoint correction terms involving Bernoulli numbers and derivatives of the summand.
short: Sums are integrals plus boundary corrections.
long: Sums are integrals plus boundary corrections. Optimally truncating the correction series often gives exponentially accurate approximations.
proof: Integrate by parts repeatedly using Bernoulli polynomials, whose derivatives differ by one.
consequence: It connects discrete and continuous analysis and supplies quadrature error expansions.

title: Poincaré Asymptotic Expansion Definition
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: A function has an asymptotic expansion relative to an asymptotic scale if the remainder after N terms is little-o of the N-th scale function as the limit is approached.
short: Asymptotic series describe limiting behaviour without needing convergence.
long: Asymptotic series describe limiting behaviour without needing convergence. The coefficients are uniquely determined once the scale is fixed, even if the series diverges.
proof: Uniqueness follows by dividing successively by the scale functions and taking limits.
consequence: It formalises the divergent expansions ubiquitous in applied mathematics.

title: Jacobi Theta Functions and Modular Transformations
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Theta functions are Gaussian Fourier series that transform under the modular inversion of their parameter with a square-root prefactor.
latex: \vartheta(z|\tau)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}e^{\pi i n^2\tau+2\pi i n z},\quad \vartheta(z/\tau|-1/\tau)=\sqrt{-i\tau}\,e^{\pi i z^2/\tau}\vartheta(z|\tau)
short: Poisson summation turns a theta series into a modular transform.
long: Poisson summation turns a theta series into a modular transform. Theta functions provide Fourier expansions of elliptic functions and heat-kernel traces on circles.
proof: Apply the Poisson summation formula to the Gaussian summands and complete the square in the Fourier variable.
consequence: It links elliptic functions, number theory, and conformal field theory.

title: Navier–Stokes Existence and Smoothness (Open)
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations with smooth initial data, global existence of smooth solutions is not known; weak solutions exist but their uniqueness and regularity remain open.
short: The fundamental regularity question for 3D fluid flow is unresolved.
long: The fundamental regularity question for 3D fluid flow is unresolved. Existence of finite-energy weak solutions was proved by Leray; the missing step is ruling out finite-time singularities.
proof: Open. Leray constructed global weak solutions via Galerkin approximations and energy estimates; whether they remain smooth is unknown, and the problem is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems.
consequence: Resolution would transform the mathematical foundations of fluid mechanics.

title: The Second Isomorphism Theorem for Groups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: If H is a subgroup and N a normal subgroup of G, then HN is a subgroup, H∩N is normal in H, and HN/N is isomorphic to H/(H∩N).
short: Multiplying by a normal subgroup and then quotienting is the same as quotienting by the overlap.
long: Multiplying by a normal subgroup and then quotienting is the same as quotienting by the overlap. The natural map h ↦ hN from H onto HN/N is a homomorphism with kernel H∩N.
proof: Define φ(h)=hN; it is surjective onto HN/N and its kernel is H∩N, so the first isomorphism theorem gives the claim.
consequence: It is the standard tool for computing quotients of products and for normaliser calculations in finite group theory.

title: The Third Isomorphism Theorem for Groups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: If N and H are normal subgroups of G with N contained in H, then H/N is normal in G/N and (G/N)/(H/N) is isomorphic to G/H.
short: Quotienting twice is the same as quotienting once by the larger subgroup.
long: Quotienting twice is the same as quotienting once by the larger subgroup. The map gN ↦ gH is well defined precisely because N is contained in H.
proof: Define φ(gN)=gH; well-definedness follows from N⊆H, and ker φ=H/N, so apply the first isomorphism theorem.
consequence: It permits iterative quotient constructions and underlies the Jordan–Hölder programme for composition series.

title: The Correspondence Theorem for Subgroups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For a normal subgroup N of G, subgroups of the quotient G/N correspond bijectively to subgroups of G containing N, preserving normality and indices.
short: Subgroups of a quotient are exactly the subgroups above the kernel, viewed from below.
long: Subgroups of a quotient are exactly the subgroups above the kernel, viewed from below. The correspondence sends K to K/N and its inverse sends L to its preimage under the quotient map.
proof: The quotient map q:G→G/N induces K↦q(K) and L↦q^{-1}(L); these are inverse because q^{-1}(q(K))=KN=K when N⊆K.
consequence: It reduces the subgroup lattice of a quotient to a segment of the original lattice.

title: The Sylow Theorems
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For a finite group of order p^n m with p not dividing m, Sylow p-subgroups exist, are conjugate, and their number is congruent to 1 modulo p and divides m.
short: The prime-power part of a finite group's order controls a rich family of conjugate subgroups.
long: The prime-power part of a finite group's order controls a rich family of conjugate subgroups. The three Sylow theorems give existence of maximal p-subgroups, conjugacy of all of them, and arithmetic restrictions on their count.
proof: Existence follows by induction on group order using the class equation; conjugacy follows from the orbit–stabiliser theorem acting on Sylow subgroups; the congruences come from counting those orbits.
consequence: They give the main structural classification of finite groups of small order and prove many groups are not simple.

title: Cauchy's Theorem for Finite Groups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: If a prime p divides the order of a finite group G, then G contains an element of order p.
short: Every prime dividing a group's order appears as the order of an actual element.
long: Every prime dividing a group's order appears as the order of an actual element. The standard proof counts tuples (g_1,...,g_p) with product 1, using a cyclic group action.
proof: Let X be the set of p-tuples with product 1 and let the cyclic group of order p rotate entries; fixed points are constant tuples, so |X| and the number of fixed points are congruent mod p, forcing a nonidentity element of order p.
consequence: It is the first major partial converse to Lagrange's theorem and a key ingredient in the Sylow theorems.

title: The Class Equation of a Finite Group
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The order of a finite group equals the size of its centre plus the sum of the indices of the centralisers of representatives of the noncentral conjugacy classes.
short: A group splits into its centre and the conjugacy classes of its noncentral elements.
long: A group splits into its centre and the conjugacy classes of its noncentral elements. Conjugacy classes partition G, and the class of x has size [G:C_G(x)] by the orbit–stabiliser theorem.
proof: Partition G into conjugacy classes; a class has size one exactly for central elements, and the other sizes are the centraliser indices.
consequence: It proves that every finite p-group has a nontrivial centre and underlies Sylow's existence proof.

title: Solvable Groups and the Derived Series
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A group is solvable if its derived series G ⊇ G' ⊇ G'' ⊇ ... reaches the trivial subgroup after finitely many steps.
short: Solvability measures how far a group is from being abelian, in finitely many commutator steps.
long: Solvability measures how far a group is from being abelian, in finitely many commutator steps. Equivalently a group has a subnormal series with abelian factor groups.
proof: The equivalence follows because a subgroup with abelian quotient contains the corresponding derived subgroup.
consequence: Solvable groups are precisely the Galois groups of polynomials solvable by radicals.

title: Nilpotent Groups and the Lower Central Series
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A group is nilpotent if its lower central series G ⊇ [G,G] ⊇ [[G,G],G] ⊇ ... terminates at the trivial subgroup.
short: Nilpotent groups are close to abelian in a stronger, central sense than solvable groups.
long: Nilpotent groups are close to abelian in a stronger, central sense than solvable groups. Every nilpotent group is solvable, but the converse fails, as the symmetric group S_3 shows.
proof: Each quotient γ_n/γ_{n+1} is abelian, giving a subnormal series with abelian factors, hence solvability.
consequence: Finite nilpotent groups are direct products of their Sylow subgroups, which makes their structure transparent.

title: The Quaternion Group as a Nonabelian Group of Order Eight
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The quaternion group Q_8 = {±1, ±i, ±j, ±k} with i²=j²=k²=ijk=−1 is a nonabelian group of order eight in which every subgroup is normal.
short: A tiny group where i times j is the negative of j times i.
long: A tiny group where i times j is the negative of j times i. It is the smallest example of a Hamiltonian group: a nonabelian group all of whose subgroups are normal.
proof: Direct multiplication of the eight symbols verifies the group axioms; ij=−ji gives noncommutativity, and every subgroup is either central or of index two, hence normal.
consequence: It shows that being a group with all subgroups normal does not force commutativity.

title: The Dihedral Groups and Symmetries of a Polygon
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The dihedral group D_n is generated by a rotation r of order n and a reflection s with srs = r^{-1}, and has order 2n.
short: Dihedral groups are the symmetry groups of regular polygons.
long: Dihedral groups are the symmetry groups of regular polygons. The relations encode that reflecting conjugates a rotation into its inverse.
proof: Every symmetry is a power of r followed by at most one reflection, giving 2n distinct elements, and the stated relations determine all products.
consequence: Dihedral groups are the standard source of small finite groups and appear throughout crystallography.

title: Simplicity of the Alternating Group A_n for n at Least Five
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For n ≥ 5 the alternating group A_n has no nontrivial proper normal subgroup.
short: Beyond degree four the even permutations form a simple group.
long: Beyond degree four the even permutations form a simple group. The proof uses that A_n is generated by 3-cycles and that any nontrivial normal subgroup contains a 3-cycle.
proof: Conjugating a nonidentity element and using commutators with 3-cycles produces a 3-cycle inside any nontrivial normal subgroup; since all 3-cycles are conjugate in A_n for n≥5, the subgroup is all of A_n.
consequence: This simplicity is the starting point of the classification of finite simple groups and explains the unsolvability of the general quintic.

title: The Sign Homomorphism and the Alternating Group
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The sign of a permutation is +1 for even and −1 for odd permutations, and defines a surjective homomorphism from S_n to {±1} whose kernel is A_n.
short: Parity of a permutation is compatible with composition.
long: Parity of a permutation is compatible with composition. A transposition has sign −1 and any permutation is a product of transpositions; the parity of the number of factors is well defined.
proof: Writing the sign as (−1)^{n−c(σ)}, where c counts cycles including fixed points, makes multiplicativity and well-definedness immediate.
consequence: The kernel A_n is a normal subgroup of index two and the foundation of determinant signs.

title: Orbit–Stabiliser for Group Actions
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For a group G acting on a set X, the size of the orbit of x equals the index of the stabiliser of x, when G is finite.
short: The number of places an element can be moved equals the number of distinct moves modulo those that fix it.
long: The number of places an element can be moved equals the number of distinct moves modulo those that fix it. The map gG_x ↦ g·x is a well-defined bijection from the coset space to the orbit.
proof: Two elements g,h send x to the same point iff h^{-1}g fixes x, i.e. iff they lie in the same left coset of G_x.
consequence: It yields the class equation, the Sylow theorems, and Burnside's counting lemma.

title: Free Groups and Their Universal Property
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The free group F(S) on a set S is generated by S with no relations beyond the group axioms, and any map S→G extends uniquely to a homomorphism F(S)→G.
short: Free groups are the most general groups generated by a given set.
long: Free groups are the most general groups generated by a given set. Elements are reduced words in the generators and their inverses, with multiplication given by concatenation and cancellation.
proof: Concatenating words and then freely reducing gives a well-defined group law; the universal property follows because a homomorphism is determined by generator images.
consequence: Every group is a quotient of a free group, which is the starting point for group presentations.

title: Group Presentations by Generators and Relations
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A presentation ⟨S | R⟩ describes a group as the free group on S modulo the normal closure of the relations R.
short: A group can be specified by a list of generators and a list of equations they obey.
long: A group can be specified by a list of generators and a list of equations they obey. The presentation formalism makes many groups compact to name, but the word problem is undecidable in general.
proof: Quotienting the free group by the smallest normal subgroup containing the relations imposes exactly those relations and no others.
consequence: Presentation theory connects group theory with topology via fundamental groups of cell complexes.

title: Ideals and Quotient Rings
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: An ideal I of a ring R is an additive subgroup closed under multiplication by arbitrary ring elements, and the cosets of I form a ring R/I.
short: Ideals are the ring-theoretic analogues of normal subgroups.
long: Ideals are the ring-theoretic analogues of normal subgroups. Closure under left and right multiplication guarantees that multiplication of cosets is well defined.
proof: If r−r' and s−s' lie in I, then rs−r's'=(r−r')s+r'(s−s') lies in I by the ideal property.
consequence: Quotient rings let one build new rings by declaring chosen elements to be zero.

title: Prime Ideals and Maximal Ideals
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A proper ideal P is prime if ab∈P implies a∈P or b∈P; a proper ideal M is maximal if no proper ideal strictly contains it.
latex: R/P \text{ is an integral domain},\quad R/M \text{ is a field}
short: Prime ideals generalise prime numbers, and maximal ideals give the largest possible quotients.
long: Prime ideals generalise prime numbers, and maximal ideals give the largest possible quotients. Every maximal ideal is prime, but the converse need not hold outside principal ideal domains.
proof: The quotient characterisations follow because R/I has zero divisors exactly when I fails to be prime and only trivial ideals when I is maximal.
consequence: The prime spectrum of a ring is the fundamental object of algebraic geometry.

title: A Quotient by a Maximal Ideal is a Field
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: An ideal M of a commutative ring R is maximal if and only if the quotient ring R/M is a field.
latex: M \text{ maximal} \iff R/M \text{ is a field}
short: Killing a maximal ideal leaves a structure in which every nonzero element is invertible.
long: Killing a maximal ideal leaves a structure in which every nonzero element is invertible. For nonzero r+M, maximality makes the ideal M+Rr equal to R, so 1=m+rr' for some m in M and r' in R.
proof: If M is maximal and r is not in M, then M+(r)=R, giving 1=m+ar and hence (a+M)(r+M)=1 in the quotient; conversely a field has no nontrivial ideals.
consequence: It produces finite fields as quotients of polynomial rings and links algebra with field theory.

title: The Isomorphism Theorem for Rings
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For a ring homomorphism f:R→S, the kernel is an ideal of R and R/ker f is isomorphic to the image of f.
short: A ring homomorphism factors through the quotient by its kernel.
long: A ring homomorphism factors through the quotient by its kernel. The map r+ker f ↦ f(r) is well defined and preserves both ring operations.
proof: The kernel is an ideal because f(ar)=f(a)f(r)=0 and f(ra)=0; the induced map is injective and surjective onto the image.
consequence: It is the basic tool for recognising quotient rings and for constructing field extensions.

title: Polynomial Rings over Fields are Euclidean Domains
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For a field K, the polynomial ring K[x] is a Euclidean domain with degree as the Euclidean function.
latex: \deg f \le \deg g \Longrightarrow \exists q,r:\ f=qg+r,\ \deg r<\deg g
short: Polynomial long division makes K[x] as arithmetic-friendly as the integers.
long: Polynomial long division makes K[x] as arithmetic-friendly as the integers. The division algorithm holds because the leading term of the divisor can repeatedly cancel the leading term of the dividend.
proof: Repeatedly subtract a suitable monomial multiple of g to lower the degree; termination gives the required quotient and remainder.
consequence: It implies K[x] is a principal ideal domain and a unique factorisation domain.

title: Gauss's Lemma on Primitive Polynomials
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The product of two primitive polynomials over a unique factorisation domain is primitive, and irreducibility over the fraction field is equivalent to irreducibility over the domain for primitive polynomials.
short: Content and primitive part let factorisation over a domain mirror factorisation over its fraction field.
long: Content and primitive part let factorisation over a domain mirror factorisation over its fraction field. The content of a polynomial is the gcd of its coefficients, and every polynomial is content times a primitive polynomial.
proof: If a prime divided all coefficients of a product of primitive polynomials, reducing modulo that prime would make one factor zero by Gauss's argument in the polynomial ring over the residue field.
consequence: It allows irreducibility tests over the integers to be carried out over the rationals.

title: Eisenstein's Criterion for Irreducibility
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: If a prime p divides every coefficient of a polynomial except the leading one, and p² does not divide the constant term, then the polynomial is irreducible over the rationals.
latex: p\mid a_i\ (i<n),\ p\nmid a_n,\ p^2\nmid a_0 \Rightarrow f \text{ irreducible}
short: A carefully chosen prime can certify that a polynomial cannot be factored.
long: A carefully chosen prime can certify that a polynomial cannot be factored. Reducing modulo p leaves a monomial, and any nontrivial factorisation would force p to divide the constant terms of both factors.
proof: If f=gh over Z, reduction mod p gives g-bar times h-bar equal to a monomial, so both factors reduce to monomials; their constant terms are divisible by p, making p² divide a_0, a contradiction.
consequence: It gives quick proofs that x^n−p and cyclotomic polynomials after substitution are irreducible.

title: Hilbert's Basis Theorem
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: If R is a Noetherian ring then the polynomial ring R[x] is also Noetherian.
short: Finitely generated ideals survive the passage to polynomials.
long: Finitely generated ideals survive the passage to polynomials. By induction, R[x_1,...,x_n] is Noetherian whenever R is.
proof: Given an ideal I in R[x], take leading coefficients of elements of I of each degree; they generate an ideal in R, and a finite set of polynomials built from generators generates I.
consequence: It guarantees that algebraic varieties are defined by finitely many equations.

title: Noetherian Rings and the Ascending Chain Condition
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A ring is Noetherian if every ascending chain of ideals stabilises, equivalently if every ideal is finitely generated.
short: Noetherian rings prohibit infinitely growing chains of ideals.
long: Noetherian rings prohibit infinitely growing chains of ideals. The equivalence relies on taking the union of a chain, which is again an ideal.
proof: If every ideal is finitely generated, a chain's union has finitely many generators all lying in one term, so the chain stabilises; the converse is similar.
consequence: Noetherian hypotheses are the standard finiteness condition in commutative algebra and algebraic geometry.

title: Localisation of a Ring at a Multiplicative Set
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For a multiplicative set S in a commutative ring R, the localisation S^{-1}R consists of formal fractions r/s with s in S, modulo the usual equivalence.
short: Localisation formally inverts a chosen collection of elements.
long: Localisation formally inverts a chosen collection of elements. When S is the complement of a prime ideal P, the result is a local ring denoted R_P.
proof: The equivalence relation is compatible with addition and multiplication, so the fractions form a ring with the universal property that elements of S become units.
consequence: Localisation is the algebraic counterpart of restricting attention to a neighbourhood of a point.

title: Fields of Fractions of Integral Domains
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: Every integral domain R embeds in a field Frac(R) whose elements are formal quotients a/b with b nonzero.
short: An integral domain can always be completed to a field by allowing division.
long: An integral domain can always be completed to a field by allowing division. Multiplication by a nonzero element is injective exactly because there are no zero divisors.
proof: Define (a,b) equivalent to (c,d) when ad=bc; the operations are well defined and give a field into which R embeds via a↦a/1.
consequence: It explains why the rationals arise from the integers and why polynomial rings have rational function fields.

title: Existence and Uniqueness of Finite Fields
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For every prime power q=p^n there exists a finite field with q elements, and any two finite fields of the same order are isomorphic.
short: Finite fields are classified completely by their number of elements.
long: Finite fields are classified completely by their number of elements. One construction takes the splitting field of x^q−x over F_p, which has exactly q roots.
proof: The splitting field of x^{p^n}−x has p^n distinct roots since the derivative is −1, and the roots form a field; any field of order q has multiplicative group of order q−1, so every element satisfies x^q=x and the field is a splitting field, hence unique.
consequence: Finite fields underpin coding theory, cryptography and the arithmetic of elliptic curves over finite fields.

title: The Frobenius Endomorphism in Prime Characteristic
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: In a ring of prime characteristic p, the map x↦x^p is a ring homomorphism; on a finite field it is an automorphism.
short: Freshman's dream is actually true modulo a prime.
long: Freshman's dream is actually true modulo a prime. All intermediate binomial coefficients are divisible by p, so they vanish in characteristic p.
proof: The binomial theorem gives (x+y)^p = sum binomial(p,k)x^k y^{p-k}, and binomial(p,k) is divisible by p for 0<k<p.
consequence: The Frobenius map generates the Galois group of finite fields and is central to arithmetic geometry in characteristic p.

title: Algebraic and Transcendental Field Extensions
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: An element is algebraic over a field K if it satisfies a nonzero polynomial in K[x], and transcendental otherwise; an extension is algebraic if all its elements are algebraic.
short: Algebraic elements are roots of polynomials; transcendental elements are not.
long: Algebraic elements are roots of polynomials; transcendental elements are not. Numbers like sqrt(2) are algebraic, while pi and e are transcendental.
proof: The subring K[α] is a finite-dimensional K-vector space exactly when α is algebraic, since it is spanned by the first degree-many powers of α.
consequence: This distinction organises field theory and underlies the impossibility of certain classical constructions.

title: Multiplicativity of Extension Degrees in Towers
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For a tower of fields K⊆F⊆L, if L/F and F/K are finite then [L:K]=[L:F][F:K].
short: Dimensions of nested field extensions multiply.
long: Dimensions of nested field extensions multiply. A basis of L over F multiplied by a basis of F over K gives a basis of L over K.
proof: If {u_i} is an F-basis of L and {v_j} a K-basis of F, the products u_i v_j span L over K and are linearly independent by comparing coordinates in the two bases.
consequence: It bounds the degree of algebraic elements and is used throughout Galois theory.

title: Constructible Numbers and Classical Compass Constructions
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A real number is constructible by straightedge and compass from a unit segment only if it lies in a field obtained by a finite tower of quadratic extensions of the rationals.
short: Constructibility is controlled by powers of two in field degrees.
long: Constructibility is controlled by powers of two in field degrees. Each straightedge-and-compass step solves at most a quadratic equation, so it at most doubles the field degree.
proof: Intersections of lines and circles require only square roots of already constructed quantities, hence successive quadratic extensions.
consequence: It proves the classical impossibility of doubling the cube and trisecting an arbitrary angle.

title: The Primitive Element Theorem
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: Every finite separable field extension is simple: it is generated over the base field by a single element.
short: One well-chosen element can generate an entire finite separable extension.
long: One well-chosen element can generate an entire finite separable extension. For infinite base fields, almost any linear combination of generators works; finite fields have cyclic multiplicative groups.
proof: Choose θ as a generic linear combination of finitely many generators so that its conjugates are distinct; the minimal polynomial then has degree equal to the extension degree.
consequence: It simplifies the study of finite extensions by reducing them to single minimal polynomials.

title: Splitting Fields and Their Uniqueness up to Isomorphism
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A splitting field of a polynomial f over K is a field extension over which f factors into linear factors and which is generated by those roots; any two splitting fields of f over K are K-isomorphic.
short: There is essentially one smallest field where a given polynomial splits completely.
long: There is essentially one smallest field where a given polynomial splits completely. Existence follows by adjoining roots inductively; uniqueness uses extension of embeddings into an algebraic closure.
proof: Any embedding of K into an algebraic closure extends step by step along adjoining roots, mapping roots of f to roots of f, hence giving an isomorphism of splitting fields.
consequence: Splitting fields are the arena in which Galois groups are defined.

title: The Galois Correspondence for Finite Extensions
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For a finite Galois extension L/K, the map H ↦ L^H is an inclusion-reversing bijection between subgroups of Gal(L/K) and intermediate fields, with [L:L^H]=|H|.
short: Subgroups of the symmetry group of a field extension correspond exactly to intermediate fields.
long: Subgroups of the symmetry group of a field extension correspond exactly to intermediate fields. Fixed fields of subgroups are intermediate fields, and the Galois condition ensures the correspondence is bijective.
proof: Artin's theorem gives [L:L^H]=|H|; taking fixed fields and groups recovers the original subgroup or field because the extension is Galois.
consequence: It translates field-theoretic questions into group theory, the central idea of Galois theory.

title: Radical Solvability and Solvable Galois Groups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A polynomial over a field of characteristic zero is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is a solvable group.
short: Radical formulas exist exactly when the associated symmetry group can be broken down in abelian steps.
long: Radical formulas exist exactly when the associated symmetry group can be broken down in abelian steps. Adjoining nth roots corresponds to cyclic extensions, and solvability corresponds to towers of such extensions.
proof: Kummer theory handles adjoining roots of unity and radicals; conversely a solvable Galois group yields a chain of cyclic extensions that are radical extensions once roots of unity are adjoined.
consequence: Since S_5 is not solvable, the general quintic cannot be solved by radicals.

title: The Normal Basis Theorem
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: For any finite Galois extension L/K there exists an element α whose Galois conjugates form a K-basis of L.
short: A single element can supply a basis consisting of all of its symmetric images.
long: A single element can supply a basis consisting of all of its symmetric images. Such a basis is called a normal basis and the element is a normal basis generator.
proof: Using the isomorphism L⊗_K L ≅ L^{G} and the structure of the group algebra as a module over itself, one finds α with linearly independent conjugates.
consequence: Normal bases are useful in computational field theory and in implementing arithmetic in finite fields.

title: Modules over a Ring as Generalised Vector Spaces
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A module over a ring R is an abelian group M with scalar multiplication R×M→M satisfying the associative, distributive and unital axioms; when R is a field this is a vector space.
short: Modules are vector spaces whose scalars form a ring instead of a field.
long: Modules are vector spaces whose scalars form a ring instead of a field. Submodules, quotients and homomorphisms are defined exactly as for vector spaces.
proof: The axioms are the vector space axioms with field elements replaced by ring elements.
consequence: Modules unify abelian groups, ideals and representations under one language.

title: Structure Theorem for Finitely Generated Modules over a PID
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: Every finitely generated module over a principal ideal domain is a direct sum of a free part and cyclic torsion parts with invariant factors dividing one another.
short: Finitely generated modules over a PID have a complete numeric classification.
long: Finitely generated modules over a PID have a complete numeric classification. The free rank and the invariant factors determine the module up to isomorphism.
proof: Use Smith normal form on a presentation matrix of the module to diagonalise the relations, giving the invariant factor decomposition.
consequence: It gives the classification of finite abelian groups and the rational canonical form of a linear operator.
wiki: Structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain

title: Schur's Lemma for Irreducible Representations
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A homomorphism between irreducible modules is either zero or an isomorphism, and over an algebraically closed field the endomorphism ring of an irreducible module consists of scalar multiples of the identity.
short: Irreducible representations admit almost no nontrivial self-maps.
long: Irreducible representations admit almost no nontrivial self-maps. The kernel and image of an intertwiner are submodules, so irreducibility forces one of them to be trivial or everything.
proof: Kernel and image are subrepresentations; if nonzero they must be all of V, making the map invertible; over an algebraically closed field an eigenvalue argument makes any endomorphism scalar.
consequence: It is the foundation of character theory and of the decomposition of representations into irreducibles.

title: Maschke's Theorem on Complete Reducibility
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite group over a field whose characteristic does not divide the group order is a direct sum of irreducible subrepresentations.
short: In characteristic zero, finite-group representations always split into irreducible pieces.
long: In characteristic zero, finite-group representations always split into irreducible pieces. Averaging a projection over the group turns any invariant complement into an equivariant one.
proof: Given an invariant subspace, average any linear projection onto it over the group action; the averaged map is a G-equivariant projection, giving a complementary subrepresentation.
consequence: It justifies the character-theoretic approach to finite group representations in characteristic zero.

title: Character Theory of Finite Groups
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The character of a representation is the function χ(g)=tr ρ(g), which is constant on conjugacy classes.
short: Characters condense whole matrices into a single class function.
long: Characters condense whole matrices into a single class function. Similar representations have equal characters, and in characteristic zero two representations are isomorphic exactly when their characters agree.
proof: The trace is invariant under conjugation, so χ is a class function; equality of characters gives equality of multiplicities by orthogonality.
consequence: Characters turn representation-theoretic questions into arithmetic with class functions.

title: Orthogonality Relations for Irreducible Characters
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: Irreducible characters of a finite group form an orthonormal basis for the space of class functions under the inner product (χ,ψ)=(1/|G|) sum χ(g) conjugate(ψ(g)).
short: Distinct irreducible characters are perpendicular in a natural inner product.
long: Distinct irreducible characters are perpendicular in a natural inner product. The number of irreducible characters equals the number of conjugacy classes of the group.
proof: Apply Schur's lemma to the matrix entries of irreducible representations, averaging over the group to obtain the orthogonality relations.
consequence: Character tables can be computed systematically and decompose arbitrary representations.

title: Decomposition of the Regular Representation
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: The regular representation of a finite group decomposes as a direct sum of irreducible representations, each occurring with multiplicity equal to its dimension.
short: The group algebra contains every irreducible representation with a predictable multiplicity.
long: The group algebra contains every irreducible representation with a predictable multiplicity. Consequently the sum of the squares of the irreducible degrees equals the group order.
proof: The character of the regular representation is |G| at the identity and 0 elsewhere; taking inner products with irreducible characters gives the multiplicities d_ρ.
consequence: It yields the fundamental identity sum d_ρ²=|G| and constrains possible character degrees.

title: The Wedderburn–Artin Structure Theorem
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: A semisimple ring is isomorphic to a finite direct product of matrix rings over division rings.
short: Semisimple rings are completely described by matrices over division rings.
long: Semisimple rings are completely described by matrices over division rings. For algebraically closed fields and finite-dimensional algebras the division rings reduce to the base field.
proof: Decompose the regular module into simple components and identify each simple Artinian ring as a full matrix ring over the endomorphism division ring of its simple module.
consequence: It classifies semisimple algebras and underlies the representation theory of finite groups.

title: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz
subject: Abstract Algebra
statement: Over an algebraically closed field, the ideals of affine space correspond to algebraic sets, and the ideal of the zero set of an ideal I is the radical of I.
short: Algebraic geometry over an algebraically closed field is a dictionary between ideals and zero sets.
long: Algebraic geometry over an algebraically closed field is a dictionary between ideals and zero sets. The weak form says every proper ideal in K[x_1,...,x_n] has a common zero when K is algebraically closed.
proof: The proof uses Zariski's lemma that a finitely generated field extension that is a field is algebraic, plus Rabinowitsch's trick to pass from the weak to the strong form.
consequence: It is the foundational theorem connecting polynomial equations with geometric varieties.

title: Multiplicativity of the Determinant
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For square matrices A and B of the same size, det(AB) = det(A) det(B).
short: The determinant converts matrix multiplication into ordinary multiplication.
long: The determinant converts matrix multiplication into ordinary multiplication. It implies that similar matrices have equal determinants and that invertible matrices have nonzero determinant.
proof: For elementary matrices the identity is checked directly; since elementary matrices generate the invertible matrices and singular products are singular, the formula extends to all A and B.
consequence: It makes the determinant a multiplicative homomorphism from the general linear group to the nonzero scalars.

title: Cramer's Rule for Linear Systems
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For an invertible square matrix A, the i-th component of the solution of Ax=b is det(A_i)/det(A), where A_i replaces column i by b.
short: Each unknown of a square linear system is a ratio of two determinants.
long: Each unknown of a square linear system is a ratio of two determinants. The formula is elegant but computationally inefficient compared with elimination.
proof: Multiplying the i-th column of A by x_i and expanding the determinant of A_i linearly in that column gives det(A_i)=x_i det(A).
consequence: It gives explicit dependence of solutions on the data and is useful in symbolic computation.

title: The Adjugate Matrix and the Inverse Formula
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For any square matrix A, A adj(A) = adj(A) A = det(A) I, so A is invertible exactly when det(A) is nonzero and then A^{-1}=adj(A)/det(A).
short: Cofactors assemble into a matrix that undoes A up to its determinant.
long: Cofactors assemble into a matrix that undoes A up to its determinant. The adjugate is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.
proof: The (i,j) entry of A adj(A) is a cofactor expansion of the determinant of A when i=j and of a determinant with a repeated row when i≠j.
consequence: It gives an explicit inverse formula and the identity det(adj(A))=det(A)^{n-1}.

title: The Laplace Expansion of a Determinant
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: The determinant of an n by n matrix equals the sum over any fixed row or column of entries times their cofactors.
short: Any row or column can be used to unfold a determinant into smaller ones.
long: Any row or column can be used to unfold a determinant into smaller ones. Repeated Laplace expansion reduces determinant computation to 2 by 2 minors.
proof: The determinant is multilinear and alternating; grouping terms by the chosen row's entry gives exactly the cofactor expansion.
consequence: It defines determinants recursively and explains their combinatorial complexity.

title: The Trace Equals the Sum of Eigenvalues
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For a square matrix over an algebraically closed field, the trace equals the sum of eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity.
short: The diagonal sum of a matrix is encoded in its characteristic polynomial.
long: The diagonal sum of a matrix is encoded in its characteristic polynomial. Similarly the determinant equals the product of eigenvalues.
proof: The coefficient of x^{n−1} in the characteristic polynomial is minus the trace and also minus the sum of its roots, which are the eigenvalues.
consequence: It gives invariant signatures of linear operators independent of basis choice.

title: The Determinant as a Product of Eigenvalues
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: The determinant of a square matrix over an algebraically closed field is the product of its eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity.
short: A matrix's volume-scaling factor is the product of its eigen-directions' stretch factors.
long: A matrix's volume-scaling factor is the product of its eigen-directions' stretch factors. The constant term of the characteristic polynomial is (−1)^n det(A), which equals (−1)^n times the product of its roots.
proof: Write the characteristic polynomial as product (x−λ_i) and compare its constant term with det(−A)=(-1)^n det(A).
consequence: It connects spectra to invertibility, volume change and the matrix logarithm.

title: Diagonalisability and the Minimal Polynomial
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: A linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field is diagonalisable if and only if its minimal polynomial splits into distinct linear factors.
short: No repeated roots in the minimal polynomial is exactly what diagonalisability means.
long: No repeated roots in the minimal polynomial is exactly what diagonalisability means. Equivalently the geometric multiplicity of every eigenvalue equals its algebraic multiplicity.
proof: The primary decomposition splits the space according to irreducible factors of the minimal polynomial; a factor (x−λ)^k with k>1 leaves a nontrivial Jordan block, while k=1 gives an eigenspace decomposition.
consequence: It gives a crisp test for diagonalisation and explains defective matrices.

title: The Minimal Polynomial Divides the Characteristic Polynomial
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For any square matrix A, the minimal polynomial m_A divides the characteristic polynomial χ_A, and both have the same irreducible factors.
short: The smallest annihilating polynomial is a factor of the characteristic polynomial.
long: The smallest annihilating polynomial is a factor of the characteristic polynomial. Cayley–Hamilton gives χ_A(A)=0, so the minimal polynomial divides it by the division algorithm.
proof: Divide χ_A by m_A to get χ_A=q m_A+r with deg r<deg m_A; evaluating at A gives r(A)=0, so minimality forces r=0.
consequence: It restricts possible Jordan forms and is central to canonical form theory.

title: The Singular Value Decomposition
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Every real or complex matrix A admits a factorisation A=UΣV* with U and V unitary and Σ diagonal with nonnegative entries called singular values.
short: Every linear map is a rotation, a stretch along axes, then another rotation.
long: Every linear map is a rotation, a stretch along axes, then another rotation. The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of A*A and are unique up to ordering.
proof: Diagonalise the positive semidefinite matrix A*A by a unitary V; set Σ to the square roots of its eigenvalues and define U=AVΣ^{-1} on the nonzero part, extending to an orthonormal basis.
consequence: It underpins principal component analysis, image compression, pseudoinverses and numerical rank estimation.

title: The QR Decomposition
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Every real matrix with linearly independent columns factors as A=QR with Q having orthonormal columns and R upper triangular with positive diagonal entries.
short: Gram–Schmidt package the orthonormalisation of A's columns into a triangular factor.
long: Gram–Schmidt package the orthonormalisation of A's columns into a triangular factor. For general matrices a rank-revealing QR with column pivoting is used.
proof: Apply Gram–Schmidt to the columns of A; the orthonormalised vectors form Q and the coefficients used form the upper triangular matrix R.
consequence: It is the standard starting point for least squares problems and eigenvalue algorithms.

title: The Cholesky Decomposition
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Every Hermitian positive definite matrix A factors uniquely as A=LL* with L lower triangular having positive diagonal entries.
short: Positive definiteness allows a symmetric square root that is triangular.
long: Positive definiteness allows a symmetric square root that is triangular. The complex analogue for positive semidefinite matrices may require a nonnegative diagonal.
proof: Construct L column by column by matching entries of LL* with those of A, using positivity to take square roots; uniqueness follows by comparing diagonals inductively.
consequence: It halve the work of solving positive definite linear systems and is widely used in Monte Carlo simulation.

title: LU Decomposition with Partial Pivoting
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: With row permutations, any square matrix can be written as PA=LU where P is a permutation matrix, L is unit lower triangular and U is upper triangular.
short: Gaussian elimination recorded as a matrix factorisation, with row swaps for stability.
long: Gaussian elimination recorded as a matrix factorisation, with row swaps for stability. Partial pivoting chooses the largest available pivot to control round-off growth.
proof: Each elimination step is multiplication by an elementary lower triangular matrix; accumulating these and the row swaps gives the factorisation.
consequence: It is the standard way to solve many systems with the same coefficient matrix.

title: The Schur Decomposition
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Every square complex matrix is unitarily similar to an upper triangular matrix whose diagonal entries are its eigenvalues.
short: Unitary changes of basis can always triangularise a complex matrix.
long: Unitary changes of basis can always triangularise a complex matrix. If A is normal the triangular factor is diagonal, recovering the spectral theorem.
proof: Choose a unit eigenvector and extend it to an orthonormal basis; the matrix becomes block upper triangular, and induction on the remaining block gives the result.
consequence: It is the theoretical basis of the QR eigenvalue algorithm and of many matrix function definitions.

title: The Polar Decomposition of a Matrix
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Every square complex matrix A can be written as A=UP where U is unitary and P is positive semidefinite, with P unique when A is invertible.
short: A matrix is a rotation composed with a stretch, in that order.
long: A matrix is a rotation composed with a stretch, in that order. The factor P is the unique positive square root of A*A.
proof: Let P=(A*A)^{1/2}; define U on the range of P by U(Px)=Ax, which preserves norms because ||Px||=||Ax||, then extend U to a unitary operator.
consequence: It generalises the polar form of a complex number and is used in continuum mechanics and quantum information.

title: The Gram–Schmidt Orthonormalisation Process
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Given linearly independent vectors, Gram–Schmidt produces an orthonormal basis spanning the same subspace by successively subtracting projections onto previously constructed vectors.
short: Subtract shadows already cast, then normalise, and repeat.
long: Subtract shadows already cast, then normalise, and repeat. In floating point arithmetic the modified Gram–Schmidt variant is more stable.
proof: Each new vector is orthogonal to all earlier ones by construction, and the span is preserved because we only subtract combinations of previous vectors.
consequence: It proves every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis and underlies QR factorisation.

title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For an m by n matrix A, the column space and nullspace of A live in R^m and R^n respectively, and the row space is the orthogonal complement of the nullspace while the left nullspace is the orthogonal complement of the column space.
short: A matrix determines two orthogonal pairs of subspaces, one in each space it connects.
long: A matrix determines two orthogonal pairs of subspaces, one in each space it connects. Their dimensions are rank, n−rank, rank and m−rank respectively.
proof: Ax=0 means x is orthogonal to every row, giving ker A=(row A)^⊥; applying the same to A^T gives the other complement relation.
consequence: This is the structural theorem behind the fundamental theorem of linear algebra.

title: The Fredholm Alternative
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For a square matrix A, the equation Ax=b is solvable for every b if and only if the homogeneous equation Ax=0 has only the zero solution.
short: For square systems, uniqueness and existence are equivalent.
long: For square systems, uniqueness and existence are equivalent. More generally Ax=b is solvable exactly when b is orthogonal to every solution of A^T y=0.
proof: The rank–nullity theorem shows that a square matrix with trivial kernel has full rank, hence its image is everything; the converse is immediate.
consequence: It is the finite-dimensional model for solvability criteria of linear integral and differential equations.

title: Sylvester's Criterion for Positive Definiteness
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: A real symmetric matrix is positive definite if and only if all its leading principal minors are positive.
short: Positivity of a quadratic form is readable from nested determinant checks.
long: Positivity of a quadratic form is readable from nested determinant checks. For positive semidefiniteness all principal minors, not only leading ones, must be nonnegative.
proof: Gaussian elimination without pivoting succeeds exactly when leading minors are nonzero; the pivots are ratios of successive leading minors and the diagonal entries of the eliminated form are positive exactly for positive definiteness.
consequence: It gives a finite test for convexity of quadratic forms and stability of equilibria.

title: Sylvester's Law of Inertia
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Under a change of basis by a nonsingular congruence transformation, a real symmetric matrix preserves the numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues.
short: The signature of a quadratic form is independent of the coordinates used to write it.
long: The signature of a quadratic form is independent of the coordinates used to write it. The triple of counts is called the inertia or signature of the form.
proof: Diagonalise the form to a sum of squares; the maximal dimension of a subspace on which the form is positive definite is invariant, and that dimension counts positive squares.
consequence: It classifies real quadratic forms and is used in optimisation and general relativity.

title: The Courant–Fischer Min–Max Theorem
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For a Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues ordered decreasingly, the k-th eigenvalue equals the maximum over k-dimensional subspaces of the minimum Rayleigh quotient, and also the minimum over codimension k−1 subspaces of the maximum.
short: Eigenvalues are optimal values of Rayleigh quotients over subspaces.
long: Eigenvalues are optimal values of Rayleigh quotients over subspaces. It extends the Rayleigh–Ritz characterisation of extreme eigenvalues.
proof: Expand in an orthonormal eigenbasis and use that any k-dimensional subspace intersects the span of the top n−k+1 eigenvectors nontrivially to obtain the upper bound, with equality for the span of the first k eigenvectors.
consequence: It justifies variational eigenvalue estimates and Weyl's monotonicity inequalities.

title: The Perron–Frobenius Theorem
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: A square matrix with strictly positive entries has a unique largest positive eigenvalue, with a positive eigenvector, and all other eigenvalues have smaller modulus.
short: Positive matrices have a dominant real eigenvalue and a positive eigenvector.
long: Positive matrices have a dominant real eigenvalue and a positive eigenvector. For nonnegative irreducible matrices the Perron root is simple and positive, with a nonnegative eigenvector.
proof: Consider the map x ↦ Ax/||Ax|| on the positive cone; Brouwer's fixed-point theorem gives a positive eigenvector, and Collatz–Wielandt inequalities give uniqueness and maximality.
consequence: It guarantees existence of stable positive equilibria in population models and underlies PageRank.

title: Gershgorin Circle Theorem
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: Every eigenvalue of a square matrix lies in the union of discs centred at a_ii with radius equal to the sum of absolute values of off-diagonal entries in row i.
short: Diagonal dominance localises eigenvalues in simple discs.
long: Diagonal dominance localises eigenvalues in simple discs. A union of k disjoint discs contains exactly k eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.
proof: For an eigenvector x with maximal component |x_i|, the eigenvalue equation gives |λ−a_ii||x_i| ≤ sum_{j≠i}|a_ij||x_j| ≤ radius times |x_i|.
consequence: It yields a quick sufficient condition for invertibility and diagonal dominance results.

title: The Matrix Exponential and Its Spectral Mapping Property
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: The series exp(A)=sum A^n/n! converges for every square matrix, and the eigenvalues of exp(A) are exp(λ) for eigenvalues λ of A.
short: Exponentiation turns additive spectral quantities into multiplicative ones.
long: Exponentiation turns additive spectral quantities into multiplicative ones. If A and B commute then exp(A+B)=exp(A)exp(B), but not in general.
proof: The series converges absolutely in any matrix norm; putting A in Jordan form shows exp(A) is upper triangular with diagonal entries exp(λ_i).
consequence: It solves constant-coefficient linear ODE systems and defines Lie group exponential maps.

title: Kronecker Products and Their Spectra
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For matrices A of size m and B of size n, the Kronecker product A⊗B has eigenvalues λ_i μ_j where λ_i and μ_j run over the eigenvalues of A and B.
short: Tensor products of operators multiply their eigenvalues pairwise.
long: Tensor products of operators multiply their eigenvalues pairwise. The determinant satisfies det(A⊗B)=det(A)^n det(B)^m.
proof: If Ax=λx and By=μy then (A⊗B)(x⊗y)=λμ(x⊗y), and eigenvectors of this form span the tensor product when A and B are diagonalisable.
consequence: It is used in quantum information, image processing and the solution of matrix equations.

title: Tensor Products of Vector Spaces and Their Universal Property
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: The tensor product V⊗W is a vector space together with a bilinear map V×W→V⊗W such that every bilinear map from V×W factors uniquely through a linear map on V⊗W.
short: Tensoring converts bilinear maps into ordinary linear maps.
long: Tensoring converts bilinear maps into ordinary linear maps. Pure tensors v⊗w span V⊗W but not every element is pure.
proof: Construct V⊗W as the free vector space on V×W modulo the bilinear relations; the universal property is immediate from the quotient construction.
consequence: It is the language of multilinear algebra, tensor fields and quantum entanglement.

title: The Double Dual and Finite-Dimensional Reflexivity
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: The canonical map V→V** sending v to evaluation at v is an isomorphism whenever V is finite-dimensional.
short: In finite dimensions, vectors are exactly the linear functionals on functionals.
long: In finite dimensions, vectors are exactly the linear functionals on functionals. The map is always injective; surjectivity fails in infinite dimensions unless extra structure is imposed.
proof: The map is injective because a nonzero vector is separated by some functional; dimensions of V and V** agree in finite dimensions, so injectivity implies surjectivity.
consequence: It justifies identifying a finite-dimensional space with its double dual and underlies reflexivity in Banach space theory.

title: Bilinear Forms and Their Gram Matrices
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: A bilinear form B on a finite-dimensional vector space is determined by the matrix B(e_i,e_j) in any basis, and the matrix in another basis is congruent to it.
short: Bilinear forms are matrices that change by congruence rather than similarity.
long: Bilinear forms are matrices that change by congruence rather than similarity. Symmetric forms can be diagonalised by congruence, and their inertia is invariant.
proof: Writing x and y in the basis gives B(x,y)=sum x_i y_j B(e_i,e_j), and a change of basis P replaces G by P^T G P.
consequence: It connects linear algebra with quadratic forms, inner products and differential geometry.

title: Symplectic Forms are Nondegenerate and Alternating
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: A symplectic form on a real vector space is a closed nondegenerate alternating bilinear form, which forces the space to be even-dimensional.
short: A symplectic form pairs directions perfectly but gives every vector zero length.
long: A symplectic form pairs directions perfectly but gives every vector zero length. Skew-symmetric matrices of odd size have determinant zero, giving even dimensionality.
proof: The matrix Ω of an alternating form satisfies Ω^T=−Ω, so det Ω = det(−Ω) = (−1)^n det Ω, forcing det Ω=0 for odd n.
consequence: Symplectic vector spaces are the linear foundations of Hamiltonian mechanics.

title: Exterior Powers and the Wedge Product
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: The k-th exterior power Λ^k V is the quotient of the tensor algebra by the relations v⊗v=0, and its dimension is the binomial coefficient n choose k for dim V=n.
short: Exterior powers measure k-dimensional oriented volume elements.
long: Exterior powers measure k-dimensional oriented volume elements. The wedge product is associative and graded commutative: α∧β=(−1)^{pq}β∧α.
proof: Alternating tensors correspond to antisymmetric multilinear maps; a basis is indexed by increasing k-tuples of basis indices, giving n choose k elements.
consequence: Exterior algebra underlies determinants, differential forms and integration on manifolds.

title: The Schur Complement and Block Matrix Inversion
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For a block matrix with invertible block A, the Schur complement S=D−CA^{-1}B satisfies det block = det(A) det(S), and the inverse can be written in terms of A^{-1} and S^{-1}.
short: Eliminating one block leaves a smaller matrix controlling the rest.
long: Eliminating one block leaves a smaller matrix controlling the rest. This is the algebraic form of Gaussian elimination on block matrices.
proof: Multiply the block matrix on the right by a suitable block triangular matrix with determinant one to block-diagonalise it as diag(A,S), giving the determinant and inverse formulas.
consequence: It appears in statistics, numerical linear algebra and computational electromagnetics.

title: The Woodbury Matrix Identity
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For invertible A and C, the inverse of A+UCV is A^{-1}−A^{-1}U(C^{-1}+VA^{-1}U)^{-1}VA^{-1}.
short: A low-rank update of a matrix inverse can be computed by inverting a much smaller matrix.
long: A low-rank update of a matrix inverse can be computed by inverting a much smaller matrix. It is also called the matrix inversion lemma.
proof: Verify by multiplying the proposed inverse by A+UCV and simplifying using the definition of the middle inverse.
consequence: It accelerates recursive least squares, Kalman filters and large-scale optimisation.

title: The Sherman–Morrison Rank-One Update Formula
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: For invertible A and vectors u,v with 1+v^T A^{-1}u nonzero, (A+uv^T)^{-1}=A^{-1}−A^{-1}uv^T A^{-1}/(1+v^T A^{-1}u).
short: Adding a rank-one term to A changes its inverse by a rank-one correction.
long: Adding a rank-one term to A changes its inverse by a rank-one correction. It is the special case of the Woodbury identity with C=1.
proof: Multiply the right side by A+uv^T and simplify, using the scalar denominator to cancel the extra term.
consequence: It enables cheap updating of inverses in quasi-Newton methods and online learning.

title: Householder Reflections for Orthogonalisation
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: The matrix H=I−2vv^T/(v^Tv) is an orthogonal reflection that maps a chosen vector to a multiple of a coordinate axis.
short: A single reflection can zero out all entries below a chosen pivot.
long: A single reflection can zero out all entries below a chosen pivot. Householder QR is numerically more stable than classical Gram–Schmidt.
proof: H is symmetric and H²=I, hence H^TH=I; choosing v=x−||x||e_1 makes Hx a multiple of e_1.
consequence: It is the standard tool for QR factorisation and tridiagonalisation in eigenvalue algorithms.

title: Companion Matrices and Characteristic Polynomials
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: The companion matrix of a monic polynomial p of degree n has characteristic polynomial p, so every monic polynomial is the characteristic polynomial of some matrix.
short: Polynomials can be realised as the characteristic polynomials of explicit matrices.
long: Polynomials can be realised as the characteristic polynomials of explicit matrices. The companion matrix has ones on the subdiagonal and negative coefficients in the last column.
proof: Expanding det(xI−C(p)) along the last column or by induction gives exactly p(x).
consequence: It links polynomial root finding to eigenvalue algorithms and proves Cayley–Hamilton in a model case.

title: A Square Matrix and Its Transpose Have the Same Spectrum
subject: Linear Algebra
statement: A square matrix A and its transpose A^T have the same characteristic polynomial and hence the same eigenvalues with the same algebraic multiplicities.
short: Taking the transpose does not change eigenvalues.
long: Taking the transpose does not change eigenvalues. The geometric multiplicities may differ, so A and A^T need not be similar over all fields in the strictest sense, though over a field they are in fact similar.
proof: The determinant is invariant under transpose, so det(xI−A^T)=det((xI−A)^T)=det(xI−A).
consequence: Row and column operations can be analysed with the same spectral tools.

title: The Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence.
short: Boundedness forces at least one accumulation point of a real sequence.
long: Boundedness forces at least one accumulation point of a real sequence. The limit point may not be unique, and the result is equivalent to the compactness of closed bounded intervals.
proof: If infinitely many terms lie at or above the midpoint of a bounding interval choose that half, otherwise choose the other half; bisecting repeatedly gives nested intervals whose lengths tend to zero, and a diagonal selection gives a convergent subsequence.
consequence: It underlies compactness arguments in analysis and the proof that continuous functions on compact intervals attain extrema.

title: The Monotone Convergence Theorem for Sequences
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A monotone increasing sequence of real numbers that is bounded above converges to its supremum, and dually for decreasing sequences bounded below.
short: Monotonicity plus boundedness is enough to force convergence.
long: Monotonicity plus boundedness is enough to force convergence. No assumption about the rate of growth is needed.
proof: Let s be the least upper bound; for any epsilon, s−epsilon is not an upper bound, so some term exceeds it and monotonicity keeps all later terms within epsilon of s.
consequence: It is equivalent to the completeness of the reals and is used to define limits of recursively defined monotone sequences.

title: Cauchy Sequences and Completeness of the Reals
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A sequence of real numbers converges if and only if it is Cauchy: for every epsilon there is N such that |x_n−x_m|<epsilon whenever n,m ≥ N.
short: In the reals, inner closeness of terms guarantees an actual limit.
long: In the reals, inner closeness of terms guarantees an actual limit. The rationals are not complete: a Cauchy sequence of rationals may converge to an irrational.
proof: Every Cauchy sequence is bounded, so Bolzano–Weierstrass gives a convergent subsequence; a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit.
consequence: Completeness is the property that distinguishes the reals from the rationals and powers fixed-point theorems.

title: The Least Upper Bound Property of the Reals
subject: Real Analysis
statement: Every nonempty subset of the reals that is bounded above has a least upper bound in the reals.
short: The reals have no gaps where a bounded set's supremum could be missing.
long: The reals have no gaps where a bounded set's supremum could be missing. This property is equivalent to completeness and to the convergence of every bounded monotone sequence.
proof: Constructed from the rationals by Dedekind cuts or Cauchy completion, one verifies that the defining cut of the supremum exists and is least among upper bounds.
consequence: It is the axiom from which the intermediate value and extreme value theorems follow.

title: The Nested Interval Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A nested decreasing sequence of nonempty closed bounded intervals has nonempty intersection, which is a single point if the interval lengths tend to zero.
short: Closed bounded intervals cannot shrink away to nothing without leaving a point behind.
long: Closed bounded intervals cannot shrink away to nothing without leaving a point behind. Closedness is essential: the nested open intervals (0,1/n) have empty intersection.
proof: The suprema of the left endpoints form a point inside every interval; if lengths tend to zero, two distinct points in the intersection would violate the shrinking bound.
consequence: It is a convenient formulation of completeness used in many existence proofs.

title: The Heine–Borel Theorem
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A subset of Euclidean space is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.
latex: K\subset\mathbb{R}^n \text{ compact} \iff K \text{ closed and bounded}
short: In finite dimensions, compact means exactly closed and bounded.
long: In finite dimensions, compact means exactly closed and bounded. The equivalence fails in infinite-dimensional normed spaces, where closed bounded sets need not be compact.
proof: Closed subsets of compact boxes are compact; for the converse every open cover of a closed bounded set can be reduced to finitely many intervals by a bisection argument.
consequence: It gives the extreme value theorem and underlies the dominated convergence arguments on compact domains.

title: The Sequential Criterion for Continuity
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A function f is continuous at a point a if and only if for every sequence x_n→a we have f(x_n)→f(a).
short: Continuity is the preservation of all convergent sequences.
long: Continuity is the preservation of all convergent sequences. In general topological spaces one needs sequences replaced by nets, but metric spaces are sequential.
proof: If f is epsilon-delta continuous, eventually x_n is within delta of a; conversely failure of continuity lets one choose a sequence x_n within 1/n of a whose images stay away from f(a).
consequence: It makes continuity easy to test using explicit sequences and explains the sequential definition of closed sets.

title: The Heine–Cantor Theorem on Uniform Continuity
subject: Real Analysis
statement: Every continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous.
latex: f\in C(K),\ K \text{ compact} \Rightarrow f \text{ uniformly continuous}
short: On a compact domain, one epsilon-delta choice works everywhere at once.
long: On a compact domain, one epsilon-delta choice works everywhere at once. The function 1/x on (0,1) shows compactness cannot simply be dropped.
proof: For each point choose a local delta by continuity; finitely many balls of half that radius cover the compact space, and a Lebesgue number argument gives a global delta.
consequence: It guarantees Riemann integrability of continuous functions on compact intervals.

title: Darboux's Theorem on the Intermediate Value Property of Derivatives
subject: Real Analysis
statement: Every derivative has the intermediate value property even when it is not continuous.
latex: f' \text{ satisfies the intermediate value property}
short: Derivatives cannot jump over values even if they are discontinuous.
long: Derivatives cannot jump over values even if they are discontinuous. This is why discontinuous derivatives, like x² sin(1/x²) at zero, must still take every intermediate value.
proof: For a value between f'(a) and f'(b), the function f(x)−cx has a local extremum in (a,b) for a suitable slope c; Fermat's theorem then gives a point where f'=c.
consequence: It shows derivatives form a restricted class of functions and motivates the study of Baire class one functions.

title: The Inverse Function Theorem in One Variable
subject: Real Analysis
statement: If f is continuously differentiable near a and f'(a) is nonzero, then f is locally invertible with differentiable inverse satisfying (f^{-1})'(f(a))=1/f'(a).
short: A nonzero derivative guarantees a local differentiable inverse.
long: A nonzero derivative guarantees a local differentiable inverse. Global invertibility needs additional hypotheses, such as strict monotonicity.
proof: The derivative's sign is constant near a, so f is strictly monotone there; applying the definition of derivative to the difference quotient of the inverse gives the reciprocal formula.
consequence: It is the one-dimensional model for the multivariable inverse function theorem and implicit function theorem.

title: L'Hôpital's Rule for Indeterminate Limits
subject: Real Analysis
statement: If f and g tend to zero or both to infinity and g' is nonzero near a, then the limit of f/g equals the limit of f'/g' whenever the latter exists.
short: For 0/0 and infinity/infinity limits, differentiate numerator and denominator.
long: For 0/0 and infinity/infinity limits, differentiate numerator and denominator. The existence of the derivative-ratio limit is required; the rule can fail without it.
proof: In the 0/0 case, Cauchy's mean value theorem gives f(x)/g(x)=f'(c)/g'(c) for some c between x and a, and then let x approach a.
consequence: It is a convenient computational tool but must be applied only to genuine indeterminate forms.

title: Upper and Lower Riemann Sums
subject: Real Analysis
statement: For a bounded function on a closed interval, the upper and lower sums over a partition use suprema and infima on subintervals; the function is Riemann integrable when their infimum and supremum over partitions agree.
short: Integrability means the best upper and lower approximations meet.
long: Integrability means the best upper and lower approximations meet. Continuous functions and monotone functions on closed intervals are Riemann integrable.
proof: Refining a partition decreases upper sums and increases lower sums; equality of the limiting values defines the integral, and the criterion follows by bounding the difference of any two sums.
consequence: It gives a precise criterion for integrability and explains why discontinuous functions may still be integrable.

title: Absolute versus Conditional Convergence of Improper Integrals
subject: Real Analysis
statement: An improper integral converges absolutely if the integral of the absolute value is finite, and conditionally if the integral converges but not absolutely.
short: Absolute convergence is robust; conditional convergence depends on cancellation.
long: Absolute convergence is robust; conditional convergence depends on cancellation. The integral of sin(x)/x from 1 to infinity converges conditionally.
proof: The inequality |∫f| ≤ ∫|f| and the Cauchy criterion for improper integrals give absolute convergence implies convergence.
consequence: It determines when rearrangement and domination arguments are legitimate.

title: Lebesgue Measure and Measurable Functions
subject: Real Analysis
statement: A Lebesgue measurable function is one for which the preimage of every Borel set is a measurable set, allowing integration with respect to Lebesgue measure.
latex: f^{-1}(B) \text{ measurable for all Borel } B
short: Measurability is the condition needed for the Lebesgue integral to make sense.
long: Measurability is the condition needed for the Lebesgue integral to make sense. Lebesgue measure extends length and is countably additive on the sigma-algebra of measurable sets.
