title: The Schröder–Bernstein Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If there are injections from A into B and from B into A, then there is a bijection between A and B.
short: Mutual embeddability of sets forces equal cardinality.
long: Mutual embeddability of sets forces equal cardinality. The proof does not require the axiom of choice.
proof: Track elements under alternating applications of the two injections; partition each set into chains and cycles and define a bijection by following the injections on one family of chains and their inverses on the rest.
consequence: It defines cardinal comparison without needing a well-ordering of the sets.

title: König's Theorem on Cardinal Sums
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If κ_i < λ_i for every i in an index set, then the sum of the κ_i is strictly less than the product of the λ_i.
short: A product of larger cardinals always outruns a sum of smaller ones.
long: A product of larger cardinals always outruns a sum of smaller ones. The special case with all κ_i finite and λ_i=2 gives Cantor's theorem.
proof: Given a map from the disjoint union into the product, diagonalise by choosing for each index a value of λ_i not used by the corresponding component.
consequence: It gives the consistency of the axiom of choice with ZF and strong inequalities in cardinal arithmetic.

title: The Hartogs Number of a Set
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: For every set A there is a least ordinal that cannot be injected into A, called the Hartogs number of A.
short: Every set has a well-ordered size that it cannot absorb.
long: Every set has a well-ordered size that it cannot absorb. Hartogs numbers exist in ZF without the axiom of choice and give the smallest well-ordered cardinal not dominated by A.
proof: Consider the set of well-orderings of subsets of A and take the supremum of their order types; the next ordinal cannot inject into A.
consequence: It is used to prove that every set can be well-ordered if and only if the axiom of choice holds.

title: Łoś's Theorem and Ultraproducts
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: In an ultraproduct of structures, a first-order sentence holds in the ultraproduct if and only if the set of indices where it holds belongs to the ultrafilter.
short: Ultraproducts transfer first-order truth from components modulo an ultrafilter.
long: Ultraproducts transfer first-order truth from components modulo an ultrafilter. Łoś's theorem is the fundamental theorem of ultraproducts and underlies nonstandard analysis.
proof: Prove by induction on formulas; atomic cases follow from the definition, boolean connectives use ultrafilter closure, and existential quantifiers use a choice function on a set in the ultrafilter.
consequence: It yields compactness, nonstandard models of the reals and transfer principles.

title: Quantifier Elimination in Model Theory
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A theory has quantifier elimination if every formula is equivalent modulo the theory to a formula containing no quantifiers.
short: Quantifier elimination reduces logical complexity to explicit conditions.
long: Quantifier elimination reduces logical complexity to explicit conditions. The theory of algebraically closed fields and the theory of real closed fields both have quantifier elimination in suitable languages.
proof: Eliminate one quantifier at a time by constructing a quantifier-free equivalent using the algebraic or order-theoretic structure, then iterate.
consequence: It yields decidability and geometric descriptions of definable sets.

title: The Tarski–Vaught Test for Elementary Substructures
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A subset A of a structure M is the universe of an elementary substructure if and only if every existential formula with parameters from A that holds in M has a witness in A.
short: Elementary substructures are exactly those that realise every existential demand they can express.
long: Elementary substructures are exactly those that realise every existential demand they can express. The test is the standard tool for building elementary chains.
proof: Induct on formula complexity; atomic and boolean cases are immediate, and the existential direction is precisely the stated witness condition.
consequence: It is used in the downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem and in model-theoretic constructions.

title: Gödel's Completeness Theorem for First-Order Languages
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A first-order sentence is provable from a theory if and only if it is true in every model of that theory.
short: Syntactic provability and semantic truth coincide in first-order logic.
long: Syntactic provability and semantic truth coincide in first-order logic. This is distinct from Gödel's incompleteness theorems, which concern the limits of particular theories.
proof: Show that every consistent theory has a model by constructing a term model from maximal consistent sets (Henkin's proof), then apply contraposition.
consequence: It legitimises model-theoretic reasoning as a substitute for syntactic derivation.

title: The Compactness Theorem for First-Order Logic
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A set of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset has a model.
short: Finite consistency is enough to guarantee an infinite model.
long: Finite consistency is enough to guarantee an infinite model. It yields nonstandard models of arithmetic and the existence of infinite models from arbitrarily large finite ones.
proof: Combine completeness with the observation that if the whole set were inconsistent, a finite subset would already be inconsistent because formal proofs are finite.
consequence: It is one of the most powerful tools in model theory.

title: The Löwenheim–Skolem Theorems
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If a first-order theory in a countable language has an infinite model, it has models of every infinite cardinality at least the size of the language.
short: First-order theories cannot control the infinite size of their models.
long: First-order theories cannot control the infinite size of their models. Skolem's paradox is that set theory has countable models even though it proves uncountable sets exist.
proof: Use the downward theorem with elementary substructures generated by a chosen subset and the upward theorem by adding fresh constants and applying compactness.
consequence: It limits the expressive power of first-order logic and is central to model theory.

title: The Deduction Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A theory proves an implication from premise to conclusion exactly when extending the theory by that premise proves the conclusion.
short: Conditional proofs correspond to proving the consequent with the antecedent assumed.
long: Conditional proofs correspond to proving the consequent with the antecedent assumed. It holds for standard Hilbert-style and natural deduction systems for first-order logic.
proof: The forward direction uses modus ponens; the converse transforms any proof from the extended theory into a proof of the implication by induction on proof length.
consequence: It is the formal justification for the everyday method of conditional proof.

title: The Soundness Theorem for First-Order Logic
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If a sentence is formally provable from a theory, then it is true in every model of that theory.
short: The proof system never proves something false in all models.
long: The proof system never proves something false in all models. Soundness is the converse half of Gödel's completeness theorem.
proof: Verify that the axioms are valid in every model and that the inference rules, especially modus ponens and generalisation, preserve truth; induction on proof length completes the argument.
consequence: It guarantees that syntactic derivation is a reliable guide to semantic truth.

title: Gentzen's Consistency Proof for Peano Arithmetic
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Gentzen proved the consistency of Peano arithmetic using transfinite induction up to the ordinal epsilon-zero, a principle not available inside Peano arithmetic itself.
short: Peano arithmetic is consistent, but proving so needs stronger ordinal methods.
long: Peano arithmetic is consistent, but proving so needs stronger ordinal methods. The result illustrates Gödel's second incompleteness theorem: the consistency statement is not provable in PA itself.
proof: Gentzen assigned ordinals below epsilon-zero to sequent derivations and showed cut elimination reduces ordinals, so an inconsistency would yield an infinite descending ordinal sequence, which transfinite induction forbids.
consequence: It founded ordinal analysis and proof theory.

title: Gentzen's Cut Elimination Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Any proof in sequent calculus can be transformed into a proof of the same sequent that does not use the cut rule.
short: Cuts can be pushed into the subproofs, yielding analytic proofs.
long: Cuts can be pushed into the subproofs, yielding analytic proofs. The subformula property of cut-free proofs gives consistency and decidability consequences.
proof: Successively reduce the complexity of cut formulas and the height of derivations by permuting cuts upward until they disappear.
consequence: It is the central theorem of structural proof theory and underlies automated theorem proving.

title: The Axiom of Regularity and the Cumulative Hierarchy
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The axiom of regularity says every nonempty set has an element disjoint from it, which forbids infinite descending membership chains and supports the cumulative hierarchy picture of sets.
short: Sets are built in layers, with no circular membership loops.
long: Sets are built in layers, with no circular membership loops. The rank of a set is the least ordinal stage at which it appears in the hierarchy.
proof: If a descending chain x_0 contains x_1 contains ... existed, the set of its members would violate regularity; conversely regularity implies every set has a rank by induction.
consequence: It gives the universe a well-founded structure enabling rank-based induction.

title: The Cauchy–Kowalevski Theorem
subject: Differential Equations
statement: For a PDE with analytic coefficients and analytic initial data on a noncharacteristic hypersurface, there exists a unique analytic local solution.
short: Analyticity guarantees local existence and uniqueness for PDEs.
long: Analyticity guarantees local existence and uniqueness for PDEs. The theorem fails in the smooth category, where the Lewy example has no solution.
proof: Rewrite the system as a majorising power series recursion; analyticity lets one bound the coefficients and prove convergence by comparison with a geometric series.
consequence: It is the PDE analogue of the Picard theorem in the analytic category.

title: Pascal's Recurrence for Binomial Coefficients
subject: Combinatorics
short: Split k-subsets according to whether they contain a fixed element.
long: Split k-subsets according to whether they contain a fixed element. The two classes correspond to choosing k-1 or k elements from the remaining n-1 elements.
proof: Fix an element x; every k-subset either contains x or does not, giving the two counts.
consequence: This recurrence generates Pascal's triangle and drives many inductive proofs.

title: Symmetry of Binomial Coefficients
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For all 0 <= k <= n, C(n,k) = C(n,n-k).
short: Choosing k objects is the same as deciding which n-k objects to omit.
long: Choosing k objects is the same as deciding which n-k objects to omit. Complementation yields a bijection between k-subsets and (n-k)-subsets of an n-set.
proof: The map A -> [n] \ A is a bijection between the two families of subsets.
consequence: It halves the computation of rows in Pascal's triangle.

title: Row Sum of Pascal's Triangle
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The entries in row n of Pascal's triangle sum to 2^n.
short: Every subset of an n-set has a unique size.
long: Every subset of an n-set has a unique size. Counting all subsets by size and by direct choice gives the identity.
proof: The binomial theorem at (1+1)^n, or counting subsets, gives the sum.
consequence: It links combinatorial counting with the algebra of the binomial theorem.

title: Alternating Binomial Row Sum
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For n > 0, the alternating sum of binomial coefficients in row n is zero.
short: Equal-weight even and odd subsets cancel.
long: Equal-weight even and odd subsets cancel. The identity is the expansion of (1-1)^n.
proof: Apply the binomial theorem to (1-1)^n.
consequence: It is the simplest example of a signed counting identity.

title: Hockey-Stick Identity
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For n >= k, the sum over j from k to n of C(j,k) equals C(n+1,k+1).
short: Count (k+1)-subsets by their largest element.
long: Count (k+1)-subsets by their largest element. The diagonal strip in Pascal's triangle sums to the entry just below its end.
proof: A (k+1)-subset of [n+1] with largest element j+1 is obtained by choosing k elements from [j].
consequence: It simplifies many sums that arise in discrete probability.

title: Counting Multisets with Stars and Bars
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of multisets of size k chosen from n types is C(n+k-1,k).
short: Place k stars and n-1 bars to record multiplicities.
long: Place k stars and n-1 bars to record multiplicities. A multiset corresponds uniquely to a nonnegative solution of x_1+...+x_n=k.
proof: Represent a solution by k stars separated into n boxes using n-1 bars, then choose the star positions.
consequence: It counts combinations with repetition and nonnegative integer solutions.

title: Multinomial Coefficients Count Ordered Group Splits
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of ways to split n labelled objects into groups of sizes n_1,...,n_m is n! divided by the product of the n_i factorial.
short: Permute all objects, then ignore order inside each group.
long: Permute all objects, then ignore order inside each group. The groups are distinguished by their prescribed sizes or labels.
proof: Choose groups successively, giving the quotient of the factorial by the internal factorials.
consequence: Multinomial coefficients expand powers of sums and model categorical counts.

title: Derangement Formula by Fixed-Point Exclusion
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number !n of permutations of n elements with no fixed point is n! times the alternating sum of 1/k! from k=0 to n.
short: Exclude every possible set of fixed points.
long: Exclude every possible set of fixed points. Inclusion-exclusion over the n possible fixed points gives the formula.
proof: Subtract permutations fixing a chosen set of k points and add back higher intersections.
consequence: It supplies the classic example of a nontrivial inclusion-exclusion count.

title: Random Permutation Fixed-Point Limit
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The probability that a random permutation of n elements is a derangement tends to 1/e as n grows.
short: The derangement sum is the truncated exponential series at -1.
long: The derangement sum is the truncated exponential series at -1. Convergence is extremely rapid, with error below 1/(n+1)!.
proof: Take the limit in the derangement formula and recognize the Taylor series of e^{-1}.
consequence: It produces the surprising e in a purely combinatorial question.

title: Ordinary Generating Functions Encode Sequences
subject: Combinatorics
statement: An ordinary generating function encodes a sequence a_n as the formal power series whose coefficient of x^n is a_n.
short: Treat a counting sequence as the coefficients of a formal series.
long: Treat a counting sequence as the coefficients of a formal series. Convergence is irrelevant when the series is used formally.
proof: By definition, coefficient extraction recovers a_n from A(x).
consequence: Algebraic operations on series become combinatorial constructions on objects.

title: Exponential Generating Functions for Labelled Objects
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For labelled structures, products of exponential generating functions correspond to splitting a label set into two disjoint parts.
short: Binomial convolution tracks which labels go to each structure.
long: Binomial convolution tracks which labels go to each structure. The division by k!(n-k)! turns the product into the binomial convolution.
proof: Choose which k labels form the first object and use the structure counts a_k and b_{n-k}.
consequence: It is the natural algebra for counting labelled combinatorial classes.

title: Cauchy Product Formula for Generating Functions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The coefficient of x^n in the product of two ordinary generating functions is the sum over k of a_k b_{n-k}.
short: A product of series counts ordered decompositions of size n.
long: A product of series counts ordered decompositions of size n. Each decomposition is determined by the size assigned to the first factor.
proof: Multiply the two sums and collect terms with total exponent n.
consequence: It converts concatenation of combinatorial classes into multiplication.

title: Generating Function for Integer Partitions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The generating function for the partition numbers is the infinite product over k of (1-x^k) to the power -1.
short: Each allowed part size contributes a geometric series of multiplicities.
long: Each allowed part size contributes a geometric series of multiplicities. Expanding the factor for k records how many parts of size k are used.
proof: A partition is uniquely specified by the multiplicities of each positive part size.
consequence: It opens the door to partition identities via generating-function algebra.

title: Euler's Pentagonal Number Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Euler product equals the alternating sum over generalized pentagonal numbers m(3m-1)/2.
short: Most coefficients cancel in the expansion of the Euler product.
long: Most coefficients cancel in the expansion of the Euler product. Only exponents of the form m(3m-1)/2 survive, with coefficient plus or minus one.
proof: It is the specialization of the Jacobi triple product, or Euler's original combinatorial involution.
consequence: It gives a fast recurrence for computing partition numbers.

title: Euler's Partition Parity Identity
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of partitions of n into distinct parts equals the number into odd parts.
short: Splitting even parts into pairs of equal parts gives a bijection.
long: Splitting even parts into pairs of equal parts gives a bijection. The generating functions are equal because (1+x^k)=(1-x^{2k})/(1-x^k).
proof: Repeatedly split each even part into two equal halves, reversing the process by merging pairs.
consequence: It is the prototype of partition identities proved by generating functions.

title: Ferrers Diagram Conjugation for Partitions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Transposing a Ferrers diagram bijects partitions with at most k parts and partitions whose largest part is at most k.
short: Reflect the diagram across its main diagonal.
long: Reflect the diagram across its main diagonal. Rows become columns, so row count and largest part swap roles.
proof: Conjugation is an involution on partitions, so it is a bijection.
consequence: Many partition identities follow by combining conjugation with other maps.

title: Partitions into Exactly k Parts
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of partitions of n into exactly k parts equals the number of partitions of n whose largest part is k.
short: Conjugate the Ferrers diagram and remove one from each resulting part.
long: Conjugate the Ferrers diagram and remove one from each resulting part. Equivalently, partitions into k parts correspond to partitions of n-k with at most k parts.
proof: Conjugating gives largest part k; subtracting one from each of the k parts gives the second form.
consequence: It lets one prove restrictions on part size or part count interchangeably.

title: Gaussian Binomial Coefficient Counts Partitions in a Box
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Gaussian binomial coefficient is the generating function for partitions fitting inside a k by n rectangle, weighted by size.
short: Lattice paths inside a rectangle are weighted by enclosed area.
long: Lattice paths inside a rectangle are weighted by enclosed area. At q=1 it reduces to the ordinary binomial coefficient counting such paths.
proof: Encode each path by the partition under it and sum q to the area.
consequence: It is the q-analogue underlying many partition and representation identities.

title: Hook-Length Formula for Young Tableaux
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of standard Young tableaux of shape lambda with n cells is n! divided by the product of all hook lengths.
short: Each cell's hook length measures how many cells constrain its label.
long: Each cell's hook length measures how many cells constrain its label. The formula connects tableaux with dimensions of irreducible representations of the symmetric group.
proof: Use the hook walk or a probabilistic argument on random corner removal.
consequence: It is central in algebraic combinatorics and representation theory.

title: Robinson-Schensted Correspondence
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Permutations of n biject with pairs of standard Young tableaux of the same shape with n cells.
short: Row insertion records a permutation as two evolving tableaux.
long: Row insertion records a permutation as two evolving tableaux. The first row of P has length equal to the longest increasing subsequence.
proof: Insert entries in order to build P and record shape changes to build Q; the process is reversible.
consequence: It links permutation statistics to tableau shapes and representation theory.

title: Fibonacci Numbers Count Board Tilings
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of tilings of a 1 by n board with squares and dominoes is F(n+1).
short: A tiling ends with either a square or a domino.
long: A tiling ends with either a square or a domino. The recurrence and initial values match the Fibonacci sequence shifted by one.
proof: Delete the last tile to get the recurrence, with T_0=T_1=1.
consequence: It gives a concrete model for Fibonacci identities.

title: Lucas Numbers Count Circular Tilings
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of ways to tile a cycle of length n with squares and dominoes is the Lucas number L_n for n at least 2.
short: Boundary dominoes split the circle into two ordinary board tilings.
long: Boundary dominoes split the circle into two ordinary board tilings. If no domino wraps around the cut, the count is a Fibonacci tiling count; otherwise it splits into two tilings.
proof: Cut an edge and separate the cases where a domino crosses the cut.
consequence: It explains the appearance of Lucas numbers in cyclic combinatorial models.

title: Motzkin Paths and Motzkin Numbers
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Motzkin number M_n counts paths from (0,0) to (n,0) with up, down, and horizontal steps that never go below the axis.
short: Flat steps are allowed in otherwise Dyck-like paths.
long: Flat steps are allowed in otherwise Dyck-like paths. Choosing the 2k up and down positions and a Dyck path of semilength k gives the formula.
proof: Select positions of nonzero steps, insert a Dyck path there, and fill the rest with horizontals.
consequence: Motzkin paths model RNA secondary structures and noncrossing partial matchings.

title: Large Schroder Numbers Count Diagonal Paths
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The large Schroder number counts paths from (0,0) to (n,n) using east, north, and diagonal steps that never rise above the diagonal.
short: Diagonal steps add a third choice to Catalan paths.
long: Diagonal steps add a third choice to Catalan paths. Substituting a Dyck path of semilength k and distributing diagonal steps gives the sum.
proof: Decompose by the number of diagonal steps and apply the Catalan count to the remaining path.
consequence: Schroder numbers appear in parsing, polygon dissections, and plane trees.

title: Narayana Numbers Refine Dyck Paths by Peaks
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Narayana number N(n,k) equals 1/n times C(n,k)C(n,k-1) and counts Dyck paths of semilength n with exactly k peaks.
short: They split Catalan paths according to their number of peaks.
long: They split Catalan paths according to their number of peaks. Summing over k recovers the Catalan number C_n.
proof: Decompose Dyck paths at peaks or use the cycle lemma on balanced words.
consequence: They refine many Catalan counts and appear in noncrossing partitions.

title: Bell Numbers Count Set Partitions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Bell number B_n is the number of ways to partition an n-element set into nonempty disjoint blocks.
short: Bell numbers aggregate Stirling numbers over all possible block counts.
long: Bell numbers aggregate Stirling numbers over all possible block counts. The first values are 1, 1, 2, 5, 15, and 52.
proof: Every partition has a unique number k of blocks and is counted by S(n,k).
consequence: They measure the number of equivalence relations on an n-set.

title: Stirling Numbers of the Second Kind Formula
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Stirling number S(n,k) equals 1/k! times the alternating sum over j of (-1)^(k-j) C(k,j) j^n.
short: Count surjections onto k labelled blocks, then forget the labels.
long: Count surjections onto k labelled blocks, then forget the labels. Inclusion-exclusion removes functions that miss at least one block.
proof: Count onto functions from an n-set to a k-set and divide by k!.
consequence: It connects set partitions with finite differences and power sums.

title: Stirling Numbers of the First Kind Count Cycles
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The unsigned Stirling number of the first kind c(n,k) counts permutations of n elements having exactly k disjoint cycles.
short: Inserting the largest element either starts a new cycle or joins an old one.
long: Inserting the largest element either starts a new cycle or joins an old one. Signed Stirling numbers carry the sign (-1)^(n-k) and are coefficients of falling factorials.
proof: Track the two insertion choices for element n and match the rising factorial recurrence.
consequence: They convert between powers and falling factorials.
wiki: Stirling numbers of the first kind

title: Exponential Generating Function of Bell Numbers
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The exponential generating function of the Bell numbers is exp(exp(x)-1).
short: A set partition is a set of nonempty sets of labels.
long: A set partition is a set of nonempty sets of labels. The EGF for nonempty labelled sets is e^x-1, and the outer SET construction exponentiates it.
proof: Apply the labelled product and SET constructions to blocks.
consequence: It is the standard example of the exponential formula.

title: Dobinski's Formula for Bell Numbers
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Bell numbers satisfy B_n = e^(-1) times the infinite sum over k of k^n/k!.
short: Bell numbers are the moments of a Poisson distribution with mean one.
long: Bell numbers are the moments of a Poisson distribution with mean one. The sum converges because factorial growth dominates any fixed power.
proof: Substitute e^x-1 into the EGF and expand exp, or use Poisson moments.
consequence: It links set partitions to probability and asymptotic analysis.

title: Lucas's Theorem on Binomial Coefficients Modulo a Prime
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For prime p, C(n,k) modulo p equals the product over base-p digits of C(n_i,k_i) modulo p.
short: Binomial coefficients factor digit by digit in base p.
long: Binomial coefficients factor digit by digit in base p. If any digit k_i exceeds n_i, the coefficient is divisible by p.
proof: Use (1+x)^n congruent to the product over digits of (1+x^{p^i})^{n_i} modulo p.
consequence: It makes binomial coefficients modulo primes easy to compute.

title: Kummer's Theorem on Carries
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The exponent of a prime p dividing C(n,k) equals the number of carries when adding k and n-k in base p.
short: Carries in base-p addition count factors of p.
long: Carries in base-p addition count factors of p. Equivalently, the exponent is the number of borrows when subtracting k from n.
proof: Apply Legendre's formula for the p-adic valuation of a factorial.
consequence: It gives a visual method for divisibility of binomial coefficients.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz
subject: Combinatorics
statement: If a polynomial has degree equal to the sum of degree bounds and the coefficient of the corresponding monomial is nonzero, then it is nonzero somewhere in any grids with more than those bounds.
short: A nonzero top monomial forces a nonzero grid value.
long: A nonzero top monomial forces a nonzero grid value. The result is Alon's polynomial method and underlies many combinatorial existence proofs.
proof: Assume f vanishes on the grid, divide by the vanishing polynomials, and compare leading coefficients.
consequence: It provides a unified tool for additive and graph-theoretic existence results.

title: Chevalley-Warning Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Over a prime field F_p, if polynomials in n variables have total degree sum less than n, then the number of common zeros is divisible by p.
short: Low-degree equations cannot have a unique or isolated solution count.
long: Low-degree equations cannot have a unique or isolated solution count. A nontrivial solution often follows when the all-zero tuple is a known solution.
proof: Sum over all points of the product of 1-f_i(x)^(p-1) and evaluate monomial sums.
consequence: It is a foundational polynomial-method tool for finite fields.

title: Erdos-Ko-Rado Theorem for Intersecting Families
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For n at least 2k, an intersecting family of k-subsets of an n-set has size at most C(n-1,k-1), with stars extremal when n is larger than 2k.
short: A largest intersecting k-family fixes one common element.
long: A largest intersecting k-family fixes one common element. At n=2k the two complementary halves give other extremal examples.
proof: Katona's cyclic-permutation method counts at most k intervals of length k in each cyclic order.
consequence: It is the starting point of extremal set theory.

title: Hilton-Milner Non-Star Intersecting Families
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For n greater than 2k and k at least 2, the largest intersecting k-family not consisting of a star has size C(n-1,k-1)-C(n-k-1,k-1)+1.
short: If no common element is fixed, one extra set is lost from a near-star.
long: If no common element is fixed, one extra set is lost from a near-star. The extremal family fixes one element in all but one set and adds a single exceptional set.
proof: Partition by a set of smallest nontrivial intersection and bound each part.
consequence: It quantifies stability of the Erdos-Ko-Rado theorem.

title: Erdos-Rado Sunflower Lemma
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every family of more than k!(r-1)^k sets of size k contains r members whose pairwise intersections are all equal.
short: Large uniform families force a family with a common core.
long: Large uniform families force a family with a common core. The common intersection is the sunflower kernel and the remaining disjoint parts are petals.
proof: Induct on k, using a maximal disjoint subfamily and counting sets meeting its union.
consequence: Sunflowers are a basic tool in extremal set theory and complexity.

title: De Bruijn-Erdos Theorem for Finite Linear Spaces
subject: Combinatorics
statement: In a finite linear space where every two points lie on exactly one line and not all points are collinear, the number of lines is at least the number of points.
short: Nontrivial finite geometries need at least as many lines as points.
long: Nontrivial finite geometries need at least as many lines as points. Equality occurs for projective planes and near-pencils.
proof: Use incidence counting and the fact that each point lies on at least two lines.
consequence: It is a foundational result of finite incidence geometry.

title: Fisher's Inequality for Balanced Designs
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A nontrivial 2-design with v points has at least v blocks.
short: The incidence matrix of a balanced design has full column rank.
long: The incidence matrix of a balanced design has full column rank. Equality characterizes symmetric designs.
proof: For the incidence matrix A, AA^T=(r-lambda)I+lambda J is nonsingular, so A has rank v.
consequence: It limits possible parameter sets of block designs.

title: Ray-Chaudhuri-Wilson Intersection Bound
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A family of k-subsets of an n-set with only s possible pairwise intersection sizes has size at most C(n,s).
short: Few intersection sizes imply few independent characteristic vectors.
long: Few intersection sizes imply few independent characteristic vectors. It generalizes Fisher's inequality and the Erdos-Ko-Rado bound.
proof: Associate to each set a polynomial that vanishes on all other sets and show their vectors are linearly independent.
consequence: It is a central linear-algebra bound for s-wise intersections.

title: Bruck-Ryser-Chowla Necessary Conditions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For a symmetric (v,k,lambda) design with v even, k-lambda must be a perfect square; when v is odd a related Diophantine equation must have a nontrivial solution.
short: Symmetric designs are obstructed by number theory.
long: Symmetric designs are obstructed by number theory. The odd case requires z^2=(k-lambda)x^2+(-1)^{(v-1)/2}lambda y^2 to have a nonzero integer solution.
proof: Analyze the rational congruence form of the incidence matrix and use Hasse-Minkowski.
consequence: It rules out many otherwise plausible design parameters, such as v=22.

title: Existence Criterion for Steiner Triple Systems
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A Steiner triple system on v points exists exactly when v is congruent to 1 or 3 modulo 6.
short: Degree and pair-count divisibility are the only obstructions.
long: Degree and pair-count divisibility are the only obstructions. Necessity follows because each point has (v-1)/2 partners and total pairs must be divisible by 3.
proof: Count incidences at a point and all pairs; sufficiency is given by explicit recursive constructions.
consequence: It completely settles a classical design-existence question.

title: Kirkman's Schoolgirl Problem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Fifteen schoolgirls can walk in rows of three for seven days so that every pair walks together exactly once.
short: It asks for a resolvable Steiner triple system on 15 points.
long: It asks for a resolvable Steiner triple system on 15 points. A resolution partitions the 35 triples into seven parallel classes of five triples each.
proof: Explicit classical constructions give such a resolvable STS(15).
consequence: It helped launch the study of combinatorial designs.

title: Mutually Orthogonal Latin Squares of Prime Power Order
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For every prime power q there exist q-1 mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order q.
short: Linear polynomials over a finite field give a full set of MOLS.
long: Linear polynomials over a finite field give a full set of MOLS. The construction is L_a(i,j)=a i+j over F_q for each nonzero field element a.
proof: For distinct nonzero a, the map j -> L_a(i,j)-L_b(i,j) is a bijection, giving orthogonality.
consequence: It supplies finite-field constructions for designs and experiments.

title: Euler's Thirty-Six Officers Problem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: There is no pair of orthogonal Latin squares of order 6, so 36 officers of six ranks and six regiments cannot be arranged accordingly.
short: The smallest order where Euler's conjecture holds is six.
long: The smallest order where Euler's conjecture holds is six. Euler had conjectured no orthogonal pair exists for any order congruent to 2 modulo 4, but orders 10 and above do have pairs.
proof: Tarry's exhaustive enumeration settles the order-six case.
consequence: It shows that small-order exceptions can mislead combinatorial intuition.

title: Finite Projective Plane of Order q
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A projective plane of order q has q^2+q+1 points and lines, each line contains q+1 points, and any two points lie on a unique line.
short: It is the incidence geometry of one-dimensional subspaces of F_q^3.
long: It is the incidence geometry of one-dimensional subspaces of F_q^3. Points and lines are the one- and two-dimensional subspaces of a three-dimensional vector space.
proof: Count subspaces and use dimension-two intersections to verify the axioms.
consequence: Projective planes supply symmetric designs and finite geometries.

title: Incidence Matrix Identity of a Projective Plane
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For a projective plane of order q with incidence matrix A, the product A times A transpose equals qI+J.
short: Two points lie together on exactly one line.
long: Two points lie together on exactly one line. The diagonal entries count q+1 lines through a point, while off-diagonal entries count one common line.
proof: The (i,j) entry counts lines containing both points i and j.
consequence: It gives an immediate spectral description of projective planes.

title: Parameter Equations for Balanced Incomplete Designs
subject: Combinatorics
statement: In a 2-(v,k,lambda) design, the replication number r and block count b satisfy vr=lambda(v-1) and bk=vr.
short: Count point-block incidences in two ways.
long: Count point-block incidences in two ways. Counting pairs containing a fixed point gives the first equation; counting all incidences gives the second.
proof: Double-count incidences and pairs of points lying in blocks.
consequence: These equations constrain all feasible design parameters.

title: Small Ramsey Number R(3,4)
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Ramsey number R(3,4) equals 9: every red-blue colouring of K_9 has a red triangle or a blue K_4, and K_8 has a colouring avoiding both.
short: Nine vertices force a triangle or a four-clique.
long: Nine vertices force a triangle or a four-clique. The lower bound uses an explicit 8-vertex colouring based on the cube.
proof: Upper bound follows from degree counting; lower bound is exhibited by a concrete colouring.
consequence: It is a classic exactly known off-diagonal Ramsey number.

title: Diagonal Ramsey Number R(4,4)
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The Ramsey number R(4,4) equals 18.
short: Eighteen vertices force a monochromatic four-clique.
long: Eighteen vertices force a monochromatic four-clique. The lower bound comes from a 17-vertex colouring; the upper bound used extensive case analysis and computation.
proof: Greenwood and Gleason gave the lower construction and an exhaustive argument for the upper bound.
consequence: It is one of the few exactly known diagonal Ramsey numbers.

title: Van der Waerden's Theorem on Arithmetic Progressions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every finite colouring of the positive integers contains monochromatic arithmetic progressions of every length.
short: Any finite colouring forces long regular patterns.
long: Any finite colouring forces long regular patterns. The proof uses induction on progression length and a notion of coloured arithmetic progressions of progressions.
proof: The original double-induction argument builds longer progressions from many shorter aligned ones.
consequence: It is a foundational result of Ramsey theory on the integers.

title: Schur's Theorem on Sum-Free Colour Classes
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every finite colouring of the positive integers yields a monochromatic triple x,y,z with x+y=z.
short: No finite colouring can make every colour class sum-free.
long: No finite colouring can make every colour class sum-free. It follows from Ramsey's theorem applied to differences, or from finite Schur numbers.
proof: Colour edges of a complete graph on (N+1) vertices by the colour of their difference.
consequence: It connects colouring to additive structure.

title: Rado's Criterion for Partition Regular Equations
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A homogeneous linear equation is partition regular over the positive integers if and only if some nonempty subset of its coefficients sums to zero.
short: A zero coefficient sum is exactly what is needed.
long: A zero coefficient sum is exactly what is needed. The criterion extends to systems via the columns condition.
proof: Necessity uses a colouring by powers of a prime; sufficiency uses the partition condition in a Rado matrix.
consequence: It classifies which linear equations survive every finite colouring.

title: Hales-Jewett Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For every alphabet size k and colour count r there is N such that every r-colouring of the Hamming cube [k]^N contains a monochromatic combinatorial line.
short: High-dimensional words force a variable-word pattern.
long: High-dimensional words force a variable-word pattern. A combinatorial line fixes some coordinates and lets the others vary together.
proof: The original proof uses induction on the alphabet and colour count with a density increment.
consequence: It implies van der Waerden's theorem and underlies density Ramsey theory.

title: Density Hales-Jewett Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every subset of [k]^N of positive density contains a combinatorial line when N is large enough.
short: Positive density is enough to force a line.
long: Positive density is enough to force a line. It is the density analogue of Hales-Jewett and implies Szemeredi's theorem.
proof: Polymath1 gave a proof using hypergraph regularity and density increment.
consequence: It unifies density and Ramsey results on words and integers.

title: Erdos-Szekeres Monotone Subsequence Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Any sequence of (r-1)(s-1)+1 distinct real numbers has an increasing subsequence of length r or a decreasing subsequence of length s.
short: Long sequences force long monotone patterns.
long: Long sequences force long monotone patterns. The bound is sharp by a standard block construction.
proof: Assign to each entry the lengths of the best increasing and decreasing subsequences ending there and use pigeonhole.
consequence: It is a classical intersection of combinatorics and analysis.

title: Mirsky's Theorem on Chain Partitions
subject: Combinatorics
statement: In a finite poset, the minimum number of antichains needed to cover the poset equals the size of a largest chain.
short: Dual to Dilworth's theorem, chains and antichains exchange roles.
long: Dual to Dilworth's theorem, chains and antichains exchange roles. Ranking each element by the longest chain ending at it gives the optimal antichain layers.
proof: The layers are antichains, and every chain meets each layer at most once.
consequence: It provides a constructive decomposition of finite posets.

title: LYM Inequality for Antichains
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For an antichain in the Boolean lattice on n elements, the sum over its members of 1 over C(n,size) is at most 1.
short: A random maximal chain meets an antichain at most once.
long: A random maximal chain meets an antichain at most once. It implies Sperner's theorem because the smallest coefficient is 1 over C(n,floor(n/2)).
proof: Choose a random permutation and count the probability that its maximal chain passes through each member.
consequence: It gives a probabilistic proof of the Sperner bound.

title: Kruskal-Katona Shadow Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Among k-uniform families of a fixed size, the initial segment in colexicographic order has the smallest possible lower shadow.
short: Packing sets as early as possible minimizes their shadows.
long: Packing sets as early as possible minimizes their shadows. The lower shadow consists of all (k-1)-subsets of members of the family.
proof: Repeated compressions move any family to a colex initial segment without increasing the shadow.
consequence: It controls face numbers of simplicial complexes.

title: Bollobas's Two Families Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: If A_i and B_i satisfy A_i intersect B_i empty and A_i intersect B_j nonempty whenever i<j, then the sum of 1 over C(|A_i|+|B_i|,|A_i|) is at most 1.
short: Cross-intersecting pairs cannot be too numerous.
long: Cross-intersecting pairs cannot be too numerous. It generalizes results about skew Bollobas systems and set-pair inequalities.
proof: Consider random permutations of each union and show the relevant orderings are disjoint.
consequence: It is a standard tool for extremal set theory.

title: Turan's Theorem on Forbidden Complete Subgraphs
subject: Combinatorics
statement: An n-vertex graph with no clique of size r+1 has at most (1-1/r)n^2/2 edges, with equality for the balanced complete r-partite graph.
short: Balanced complete multipartite graphs are extremal.
long: Balanced complete multipartite graphs are extremal. The exact extremal graph is the Turan graph T_r(n).
proof: Zykov symmetrization turns any extremal graph into a complete multipartite one, then balancing parts maximizes edges.
consequence: It begins extremal graph theory and quantifies clique avoidance.

title: Mantel's Triangle-Free Edge Bound
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A triangle-free graph on n vertices has at most floor(n^2/4) edges.
short: The complete bipartite graph is the best triangle-free choice.
long: The complete bipartite graph is the best triangle-free choice. It is the case r=2 of Turan's theorem.
proof: For each edge uv, degrees d(u)+d(v)<=n; summing over edges and applying Cauchy-Schwarz gives the bound.
consequence: It is the oldest extremal graph theorem.

title: Kovari-Sos-Turan Bound for Bipartite Forbidden Graphs
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For s at most t, the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex graph with no K_{s,t} is at most O(n^{2-1/s}).
short: Counting common neighbours bounds bipartite subgraph density.
long: Counting common neighbours bounds bipartite subgraph density. The order is correct when t is large enough relative to s.
proof: Double-count pairs consisting of an s-set of vertices and a common neighbour, using convexity.
consequence: It covers extremal problems that Turan's theorem cannot resolve.

title: Szemeredi Regularity Lemma
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every large graph admits a partition into a bounded number of parts such that almost every pair of parts behaves pseudorandomly.
latex: \forall\varepsilon\;\exists M:\text{}\varepsilon\text{-regular partition with at most }M\text{ parts}
short: Large graphs can be approximated by weighted random-looking graphs.
long: Large graphs can be approximated by weighted random-looking graphs. A pair is epsilon-regular if edge densities between all sufficiently large subparts are close.
proof: Refine partitions whenever irregular pairs remain; a mean-square density potential strictly increases.
consequence: It underlies the graph removal lemma and property testing.

title: Graph Removal Lemma
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For every fixed graph H and tolerance epsilon, a graph with few copies of H can be made H-free by deleting at most epsilon n^2 edges.
short: Few forbidden subgraphs can be destroyed cheaply.
long: Few forbidden subgraphs can be destroyed cheaply. It follows from the regularity lemma and the counting lemma.
proof: Regularize the graph, remove edges inside parts and between irregular or forbidden-density pairs.
consequence: It gives deletion versions of many extremal results and underlies property testing.

title: Graham-Pollak Biclique Partition Bound
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Partitioning the edge set of the complete graph on n vertices into complete bipartite subgraphs requires at least n-1 subgraphs.
short: Linear algebra forces many bicliques.
long: Linear algebra forces many bicliques. The decomposition into stars shows n-1 is attainable.
proof: Assign a real variable to each vertex and use the linear independence of the corresponding rank-one matrices.
consequence: It is a classic algebraic lower bound in combinatorics.

title: Rank Sizes of the Boolean Lattice
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The number of k-element subsets of an n-element set is C(n,k), so the rank sizes of the Boolean lattice are binomial coefficients.
short: The k-th layer consists of all k-subsets.
long: The k-th layer consists of all k-subsets. The total number of elements in the Boolean lattice is 2^n.
proof: By definition, a k-subset is chosen by selecting k of n elements.
consequence: It makes the Boolean lattice the basic example of a graded poset.

title: Mobius Function of the Boolean Lattice
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For subsets S contained in T, the poset Mobius function equals (-1) to the size of T minus S.
short: Alternating signs cancel over intermediate subsets.
long: Alternating signs cancel over intermediate subsets. It is the poset analogue of the classical number-theoretic Mobius inversion.
proof: The defining recurrence sums (-1)^j C(|T|-|S|,j), which is zero unless S=T.
consequence: It yields inclusion-exclusion as a special case of poset inversion.

title: Incidence Algebra and Zeta Inversion
subject: Combinatorics
statement: The incidence algebra of a locally finite poset has convolution as product, and the inverse of the zeta function is the Mobius function.
short: Poset inversion generalizes summation by parts.
long: Poset inversion generalizes summation by parts. The zeta function is 1 on every comparable pair and its convolution inverse is mu.
proof: The recursive definition of mu is exactly the equation zeta * mu = delta.
consequence: It unifies many inversion formulas on partially ordered sets.

title: Every Finite Nonempty Poset Has a Minimal Element
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every nonempty finite partially ordered set contains at least one minimal element.
short: Following a descending chain must stop.
long: Following a descending chain must stop. There may be several minimal elements, and they need not be comparable.
proof: Start anywhere and move to a smaller element until no smaller element exists; finiteness forces termination.
consequence: It underlies greedy algorithms and inductive arguments on posets.

title: Knaster-Tarski Fixed-Point Theorem
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Every monotone function on a complete lattice has a fixed point, and its fixed points form a complete lattice.
short: Monotone self-maps cannot avoid fixed points.
long: Monotone self-maps cannot avoid fixed points. The least fixed point is the infimum of all pre-fixed points.
proof: Take the infimum of the set of x with f(x)<=x and use monotonicity to show it is fixed.
consequence: It justifies least fixed-point semantics and closure constructions.

title: Galois Connections Between Posets
subject: Combinatorics
statement: An adjoint pair of monotone maps between posets satisfies f(x)<=y exactly when x<=g(y); the composites are closure operators.
short: Adjoints translate inequalities across two worlds.
long: Adjoints translate inequalities across two worlds. Every closure operator arises from such a connection in a standard way.
proof: Apply the adjunction twice to show x<=g(f(x)) and f(g(y))<=y, giving idempotent composites.
consequence: Galois connections appear in algebra, topology, and logic.

title: Mobius Function of the Partition Lattice
subject: Combinatorics
statement: For the lattice of set partitions ordered by refinement, the Mobius function from the bottom element to a partition is the product over blocks of (-1) to the block size minus one times the factorial of block size minus one.
short: Each block contributes an independent sign and factorial.
long: Each block contributes an independent sign and factorial. For the one-block partition this recovers the inclusion-exclusion count of surjections.
proof: Use the crosscut theorem or compute by induction on the number of blocks.
consequence: It supports Mobius inversion on partition lattices.

title: Sauer-Shelah Lemma on VC Dimension
subject: Combinatorics
statement: A family of subsets of an n-element set with VC dimension at most d has size at most the sum over i up to d of C(n,i).
short: Low shattering dimension limits family size polynomially.
long: Low shattering dimension limits family size polynomially. The bound is attained by all subsets of size at most d.
proof: Induct on n and d by splitting the family according to whether sets contain a fixed element.
consequence: It is the combinatorial foundation of statistical learning theory.

title: Union-Closed Sets Conjecture
subject: Combinatorics
statement: Open: every finite union-closed family of sets other than the trivial family has an element belonging to at least half of its members.
short: An element should appear in at least half the sets.
long: An element should appear in at least half the sets. The conjecture remains open in general, though it is known for families with small sets and for many lattice cases.
proof: Open. No general proof is known; partial results use lattice theory and compressor arguments.
consequence: It is a famously simple-looking open problem in extremal set theory.

title: Tree Characterization by Edge Count
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A connected graph on n vertices is a tree if and only if it has exactly n-1 edges.
short: A tree is a minimally connected graph.
long: A tree is a minimally connected graph. Any connected graph has a spanning tree, and extra edges create cycles.
proof: Remove cycle edges until acyclic; the resulting spanning tree has n-1 edges by induction.
consequence: It gives a quick test for tree structure.

title: Every Tree Has at Least Two Leaves
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Every tree with at least two vertices has at least two vertices of degree one.
short: The ends of a longest path are leaves.
long: The ends of a longest path are leaves. A single-vertex tree is the only tree without a degree-one vertex.
proof: Take a longest path; if an endpoint had another neighbour, the path could be extended or would create a cycle.
consequence: Leaf existence supports pruning algorithms and tree induction.

title: Prufer Sequence Bijection for Labelled Trees
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Labelled trees on n vertices biject with sequences of length n-2 over the label set.
short: Repeatedly delete the smallest leaf to encode a tree.
long: Repeatedly delete the smallest leaf to encode a tree. The decoding algorithm reconstructs the tree by joining each sequence entry to the smallest absent label.
proof: Leaf deletion and its reverse are inverse maps, giving the bijection and Cayley's count.
consequence: It yields Cayley's formula and useful random-tree models.

title: Forest Edge Count by Components
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A forest with n vertices and c connected components has exactly n-c edges.
short: Each tree component with v_i vertices has v_i-1 edges.
long: Each tree component with v_i vertices has v_i-1 edges. Summing over components gives n minus the number of components.
proof: Apply the tree edge count to each component and sum.
consequence: It generalizes the tree edge count and tracks component changes.

title: Dimension of the Cycle Space
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The cycle space of a graph with n vertices, m edges, and c components has dimension m-n+c over the two-element field.
short: Each independent cycle adds one degree of freedom.
long: Each independent cycle adds one degree of freedom. It is also called the cyclomatic number or first Betti number of the graph.
proof: A spanning forest has n-c edges; each remaining edge creates one independent fundamental cycle.
consequence: It links graph theory with homology and network analysis.

title: Cut Space Is Orthogonal to Cycle Space
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Over the two-element field, every edge cut vector has even intersection with every cycle vector.
short: A cycle crosses any cut an even number of times.
long: A cycle crosses any cut an even number of times. This orthogonality explains the decomposition of the edge space into cut and cycle parts.
proof: Travel around a cycle; each time it crosses the cut it must later cross back.
consequence: It is the graph-theoretic basis of Kirchhoff's circuit laws.

title: Planar Graph Edge Bound for Simple Graphs
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A simple planar graph with n at least 3 has at most 3n-6 edges, and a triangle-free planar graph has at most 2n-4 edges.
short: Euler's formula and face lengths limit density.
long: Euler's formula and face lengths limit density. Equality holds for triangulations and for quadrangulations respectively.
proof: Each face has length at least 3, or 4 in the triangle-free case, and each edge borders two face sides.
consequence: It quickly proves nonplanarity of dense graphs.

title: Nonplanarity of K5 and K3,3
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The complete graph K5 and the complete bipartite graph K3,3 are not planar.
short: Both violate the planar edge or face-length bounds.
long: Both violate the planar edge or face-length bounds. K5 has too many edges, while K3,3 is bipartite with too many edges for a quadrangulation.
proof: Apply m<=3n-6 to K5 and m<=2n-4 to K3,3.
consequence: They are the two forbidden building blocks in Kuratowski's theorem.

title: Kuratowski's Planarity Criterion
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A finite graph is planar if and only if it contains no subdivision of K5 or K3,3.
short: Planarity is characterized by two forbidden topological subgraphs.
long: Planarity is characterized by two forbidden topological subgraphs. A subdivision replaces edges by internally disjoint paths.
proof: The hard direction analyzes a minimal nonplanar graph and reconstructs a subdivision.
consequence: It gives a structural, although not efficient, planarity test.

title: Wagner's Minor Criterion for Planarity
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A finite graph is planar if and only if it has neither K5 nor K3,3 as a minor.
short: Forbidden minors characterize planarity.
long: Forbidden minors characterize planarity. Unlike subdivisions, minors allow contracting edges as well as deleting them.
proof: Kuratowski's subdivisions yield minors, and the converse follows by analyzing minor-minimal obstructions.
consequence: It is a precursor to the general graph minor theory.

title: Dirac's Minimum-Degree Hamiltonicity Condition
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A simple graph on n at least 3 vertices with minimum degree at least n/2 contains a Hamiltonian cycle.
short: Large minimum degree forces a spanning cycle.
long: Large minimum degree forces a spanning cycle. The bound is sharp: two cliques sharing one vertex fail just below it.
proof: Take a longest path; its endpoints have neighbours on the path that allow insertion into a cycle through all vertices.
consequence: It is the first major sufficient condition for Hamiltonicity.

title: Ore's Degree-Sum Hamiltonicity Condition
subject: Graph Theory
statement: If every pair of nonadjacent vertices in an n-vertex simple graph has degree sum at least n, then the graph is Hamiltonian.
short: Nonedges cannot have too small combined degree.
long: Nonedges cannot have too small combined degree. Dirac's condition implies Ore's condition.
proof: Close the graph by repeatedly adding edges between nonadjacent pairs of degree sum at least n until it is complete or Hamiltonian.
consequence: It generalizes Dirac's theorem.

title: Chvatal-Erdos Connectivity Condition
subject: Graph Theory
statement: If the vertex connectivity of a graph is at least its independence number, then the graph is Hamiltonian.
short: Connectivity that dominates independence forces a spanning cycle.
long: Connectivity that dominates independence forces a spanning cycle. It applies to many dense graphs with limited independent sets.
proof: A longest cycle leaving vertices outside yields an independent set whose size exceeds connectivity, a contradiction.
consequence: It links three fundamental graph invariants.

title: Bondy-Chvatal Closure
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Adding an edge between nonadjacent vertices whose degree sum is at least n preserves Hamiltonicity.
latex: d(u)+d(v)\ge n\Rightarrow G+uv\text{ Hamiltonian iff }G\text{ is}
short: Degree-sum closure changes no Hamiltonicity information.
long: Degree-sum closure changes no Hamiltonicity information. The iterative closure is unique and decides Hamiltonicity in some graph classes.
proof: If a Hamiltonian cycle uses the new edge, the degree-sum condition inserts u and v into a spanning path of the original graph.
consequence: It unifies Ore-type arguments.

title: Grotzsch's Three-Colour Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Every triangle-free planar graph is 3-colourable.
short: Removing triangles improves the planar colour bound.
long: Removing triangles improves the planar colour bound. It cannot be extended to nonplanar triangle-free graphs, which may have arbitrarily large chromatic number.
proof: A minimal counterexample is shown to be critical; discharging rules give a contradiction.
consequence: It refines the Four Colour Theorem in the triangle-free case.

title: Brooks' Colouring Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A connected graph with maximum degree Delta has chromatic number at most Delta unless it is a complete graph or an odd cycle.
short: Greedy colouring is almost optimal.
long: Greedy colouring is almost optimal. The exceptions require Delta+1 colours only for cliques and odd cycles.
proof: Order vertices suitably and greedily colour; connected non-exception graphs admit a spanning order where each vertex has a later neighbour.
consequence: It sharpens the trivial greedy bound.

title: Five Colour Theorem for Planar Graphs
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Every planar graph can be coloured with five colours.
short: Kempe chains give a simple inductive colouring.
long: Kempe chains give a simple inductive colouring. It is weaker than the Four Colour Theorem but much easier to prove.
proof: In a minimal counterexample, find a vertex of degree at most five and recolour using Kempe chains.
consequence: It was the classical stepping stone to the Four Colour Theorem.

title: Perfect Graph Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A graph is perfect exactly when its complement is perfect.
short: Perfection is inherited by complements.
long: Perfection is inherited by complements. In a perfect graph every induced subgraph has chromatic number equal to clique number.
proof: Lovasz proved the replication lemma and used it to establish complement invariance.
consequence: It explains symmetry between clique covers and colourings.

title: Strong Perfect Graph Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A graph is perfect if and only if it has no induced odd cycle of length at least five and no complement of such a cycle.
latex: G\text{ perfect}\iff\text{no odd holes or antiholes}
short: Odd holes and their complements are the only obstructions.
long: Odd holes and their complements are the only obstructions. The result resolved a long-standing conjecture of Berge.
proof: Chudnovsky, Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas gave a structural proof using decomposition of imperfect graphs.
consequence: It characterizes perfection by a list of forbidden induced subgraphs.

title: Koning's Matching-Vertex-Cover Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: In a bipartite graph, the maximum matching size equals the minimum vertex cover size.
short: Bipartite matchings and covers are dual.
long: Bipartite matchings and covers are dual. It fails for general graphs, where only the inequality nu <= tau holds.
proof: Use alternating paths from unmatched vertices to construct a cover of size equal to the matching.
consequence: It is the graph analogue of linear programming duality.

title: Hall's Marriage Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A bipartite graph has a matching saturating one side if and only if every subset of that side has at least as many neighbours as it has vertices.
short: No subset of suitors can be short of choices.
long: No subset of suitors can be short of choices. The condition is clearly necessary and, surprisingly, sufficient.
proof: If Hall's condition fails, no matching exists; otherwise induction or alternating paths build one.
consequence: It has countless applications to systems of distinct representatives.

title: Tutte's Perfect Matching Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A graph has a perfect matching if and only if for every vertex subset S, the number of odd components of G-S is at most the size of S.
short: Odd components must be certified by removed vertices.
long: Odd components must be certified by removed vertices. It generalizes Hall's theorem to arbitrary graphs.
proof: Necessity is immediate; sufficiency follows from Tutte's matrix or Gallai-Edmonds decomposition.
consequence: It gives a complete structural criterion for perfect matchings.

title: Berge's Augmenting Path Criterion
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A matching is maximum if and only if there is no augmenting path relative to it.
short: An augmenting path is exactly a way to improve a matching.
long: An augmenting path is exactly a way to improve a matching. It underlies most matching algorithms.
proof: The symmetric difference of two matchings decomposes into alternating paths and cycles; a larger matching yields an augmenting path.
consequence: It reduces optimization to searching for a structural witness.

title: Edmonds' Blossom Algorithm
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The blossom algorithm finds a maximum matching in a general graph in polynomial time by contracting odd cycles called blossoms.
short: Odd cycles are handled by shrinking them temporarily.
long: Odd cycles are handled by shrinking them temporarily. It extends bipartite augmenting-path search to nonbipartite graphs.
proof: Contracting a blossom preserves the existence of an augmenting path; contraction and expansion can be managed efficiently.
consequence: It solved the general matching problem algorithmically.

title: Hungarian Algorithm for the Assignment Problem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The Hungarian algorithm solves the minimum-cost perfect matching problem in a bipartite graph in cubic time.
short: Dual potentials turn assignment into repeated augmentations.
long: Dual potentials turn assignment into repeated augmentations. It is equivalent to finding a minimum-weight perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph.
proof: Maintain feasible dual potentials and complementary slackness while growing alternating trees.
consequence: It is a classic polynomial-time optimization algorithm.

title: Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem for Networks
subject: Graph Theory
statement: In a capacitated network, the maximum value of an s-t flow equals the minimum capacity of an s-t cut.
short: The bottleneck capacity is exactly achievable.
long: The bottleneck capacity is exactly achievable. The residual graph certifies optimality when no augmenting path remains.
proof: Ford-Fulkerson finds a flow whose residual network has no s-t path; reachable vertices define a cut of equal capacity.
consequence: It unifies network flow, connectivity, and matching algorithms.

title: Menger's Theorem on Vertex Connectivity
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint paths between two nonadjacent vertices equals the minimum number of vertices whose removal separates them.
short: Disjoint paths and separating sets are dual.
long: Disjoint paths and separating sets are dual. The edge version is analogous with edge cuts.
proof: Model vertex capacities by splitting vertices and apply max-flow min-cut.
consequence: It gives a structural interpretation of connectivity.

title: Edge Version of Menger's Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The maximum number of edge-disjoint paths between two vertices equals the minimum size of an edge cut separating them.
short: Edge-disjoint routes match edge bottlenecks.
long: Edge-disjoint routes match edge bottlenecks. It follows from max-flow min-cut with unit edge capacities.
proof: Assign capacity one to each edge; integral maximum flow decomposes into edge-disjoint paths.
consequence: It underlies network reliability and cut algorithms.

title: Integrality of Maximum Flows
subject: Graph Theory
statement: If all capacities are integers, there is a maximum flow taking only integer values on every edge.
short: Integer capacities never require fractional flows.
long: Integer capacities never require fractional flows. It is essential for combinatorial applications such as matching.
proof: Ford-Fulkerson augments by integer bottleneck amounts, preserving integrality at every step.
consequence: It converts continuous flow results into discrete algorithms.

title: Gomory-Hu Cut Tree
subject: Graph Theory
statement: An undirected weighted graph has a weighted tree on the same vertices that represents all pairwise minimum cut values.
short: One tree encodes every pairwise bottleneck.
long: One tree encodes every pairwise bottleneck. The minimum edge on the tree path gives the pair's minimum cut value.
proof: Repeatedly split the vertex set by a minimum cut and recurse on the two sides.
consequence: It compresses n choose k pairwise cut computations.

title: Eulerian Circuit Degree Criterion
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A connected graph has a closed trail using every edge exactly once if and only if every vertex has even degree.
short: Every arrival must have a matching departure.
long: Every arrival must have a matching departure. An open Euler trail exists exactly when zero or two vertices have odd degree.
proof: Necessity is immediate; sufficiency follows by splicing closed cycles at repeated vertices.
consequence: It solves the classical route-inspection question.

title: Hierholzer's Algorithm for Eulerian Circuits
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Hierholzer's algorithm constructs an Eulerian circuit by splicing cycles in linear time.
short: Keep splicing cycles until no unused edges remain.
long: Keep splicing cycles until no unused edges remain. The algorithm maintains a current trail and inserts detours when a vertex repeats.
proof: Every spliced detour starts and ends at the same vertex, so the trail remains a closed trail.
consequence: It is the standard efficient construction of Euler tours.

title: Chinese Postman Problem on Undirected Graphs
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A shortest closed walk covering every edge is obtained by pairing odd-degree vertices with minimum-weight perfect matching and duplicating the corresponding shortest paths.
short: Make all degrees even as cheaply as possible.
long: Make all degrees even as cheaply as possible. The resulting multigraph has an Euler circuit giving the postman tour.
proof: Odd-degree vertices must occur an even number of times in any Eulerization, and shortest paths give the cheapest pairing.
consequence: It models mail delivery and route planning.

title: Bridge Detection with DFS Low Links
subject: Graph Theory
statement: In a depth-first search tree, a tree edge to vertex v is a bridge exactly when the low-link value of v exceeds the discovery time of its parent.
short: No back edge from the subtree reaches above the parent.
long: No back edge from the subtree reaches above the parent. The test runs in linear time.
proof: The subtree separated by the edge has no edge to the discovered ancestors, so removing it disconnects the graph.
consequence: It is a standard reachability diagnostic.

title: Articulation Point Detection with Low Links
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A nonroot vertex in a DFS tree is an articulation point if and only if some child has low-link value at least its discovery time.
short: A child subtree cannot reach above the vertex.
long: A child subtree cannot reach above the vertex. The root is an articulation point exactly when it has more than one DFS child.
proof: If the child's subtree has no back edge above v, deleting v separates that subtree.
consequence: It identifies cut vertices in linear time.

title: Kosaraju's Strongly Connected Components Algorithm
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Strongly connected components can be found by depth-first search order followed by search on the reversed graph.
short: Process vertices in decreasing finishing time on the reverse graph.
long: Process vertices in decreasing finishing time on the reverse graph. Each tree in the second pass is exactly one strongly connected component.
proof: The condensation graph is a DAG, and the finishing order makes source components appear first.
consequence: It is a simple linear-time SCC algorithm.

title: Tarjan's Strongly Connected Components Algorithm
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Tarjan's algorithm outputs a strongly connected component whenever a DFS root has low-link value equal to its discovery time.
short: Stack entries above a low-link root form one component.
long: Stack entries above a low-link root form one component. It needs only one pass and uses a stack of active vertices.
proof: At such a root, the stack portion cannot reach an earlier vertex and is mutually reachable.
consequence: It is the standard one-pass SCC algorithm.

title: Dijkstra's Shortest-Path Algorithm
subject: Graph Theory
statement: With nonnegative edge weights, repeatedly fixing the closest unvisited vertex yields shortest paths from a source.
short: Once a vertex is extracted, its distance cannot improve.
long: Once a vertex is extracted, its distance cannot improve. With a binary heap the standard running time is as shown.
proof: If a shorter path existed, its predecessor on the path would have been extracted earlier with a smaller distance.
consequence: It is the default shortest-path algorithm for nonnegative weights.

title: Bellman-Ford Algorithm and Negative Cycles
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Relaxing every edge n-1 times computes single-source shortest paths with negative edges and detects any negative cycle by one further relaxation.
short: Simple paths have at most n-1 edges.
long: Simple paths have at most n-1 edges. A further improvement after n-1 rounds signals a reachable negative cycle.
proof: Induct on the maximum number of edges in a shortest path.
consequence: It handles weights that Dijkstra's algorithm cannot.

title: Floyd–Warshall Algorithm for All-Pairs Shortest Paths
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Dynamic programming over allowed intermediate vertices computes all-pairs shortest paths in O(n^3) time.
short: Allow one more vertex as an intermediate stop.
long: Allow one more vertex as an intermediate stop. It also works with negative edges as long as there is no negative cycle.
proof: Induct on the set of permitted intermediate vertices.
consequence: It is simple and suitable for dense graphs.

title: Kruskal's Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithm
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Sorting edges by weight and adding an edge whenever it joins different components produces a minimum spanning tree.
short: Always take the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle.
long: Always take the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle. A union-find structure tracks the growing components.
proof: The cut property shows each chosen edge is safe for some minimum spanning tree.
consequence: It is a classic greedy algorithm with a full correctness proof.

title: Prim's Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithm
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Growing a tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge leaving it produces a minimum spanning tree.
short: Expand the current tree along its cheapest frontier edge.
long: Expand the current tree along its cheapest frontier edge. It is analogous to Dijkstra's algorithm but uses edge weights rather than path lengths.
proof: Every chosen edge is lightest across the cut defined by the current tree.
consequence: It is efficient on dense graphs with a priority queue.

title: The Cut Property of Minimum Spanning Trees
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some minimum spanning tree, and if its weight is strictly smallest it belongs to every one.
short: Cheapest crossing edges are always safe.
long: Cheapest crossing edges are always safe. It justifies both Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms.
proof: Exchange an edge of a spanning tree that crosses the same cut with the lighter edge.
consequence: It is the central correctness lemma for MST algorithms.

title: The Cycle Property of Minimum Spanning Trees
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A heaviest edge on any cycle is excluded from some minimum spanning tree, and if its weight is strictly largest it is excluded from every one.
latex: e\text{ heavy on cycle}\Rightarrow e\notin MST
short: Avoid the most expensive edge of a cycle.
long: Avoid the most expensive edge of a cycle. It is the cycle dual of the cut property.
proof: Removing e from any spanning tree containing it splits the cycle, and another cycle edge reconnects the parts more cheaply.
consequence: It supports deletion-based MST algorithms.

title: Matrix-Tree Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Any cofactor of the graph Laplacian equals the number of spanning trees of the graph.
short: A determinant counts spanning trees.
long: A determinant counts spanning trees. The Laplacian is the degree matrix minus the adjacency matrix.
proof: Use the incidence matrix and Cauchy-Binet to expand the cofactor as a sum over spanning forests.
consequence: It links spectral graph theory with enumeration.

title: Laplacian Spectrum of the Complete Graph
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The Laplacian eigenvalues of K_n are 0 with multiplicity one and n with multiplicity n-1.
short: The all-ones vector and its orthogonal complement diagonalize the Laplacian.
long: The all-ones vector and its orthogonal complement diagonalize the Laplacian. It gives tau(K_n)=n^{n-2} via the Matrix-Tree Theorem.
proof: Since L=nI-J, vectors orthogonal to the all-ones vector have eigenvalue n and the constant vector has eigenvalue 0.
consequence: It is the simplest nontrivial Laplacian spectrum.

title: Adjacency Spectrum of a Cycle
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The adjacency eigenvalues of the n-cycle are 2 times the cosine of 2 pi j/n for j from 0 to n-1.
short: Discrete Fourier modes diagonalize a cycle.
long: Discrete Fourier modes diagonalize a cycle. The largest eigenvalue is 2, and for even n the smallest is -2.
proof: Apply the adjacency matrix to a complex exponential vector supported cyclically.
consequence: It is the starting example for spectral analysis of regular graphs.

title: Cheeger's Inequality for Graphs
subject: Graph Theory
statement: For a graph with normalized Laplacian spectral gap lambda and conductance h, lambda/2 is at most h and h is at most the square root of 2 lambda.
short: Spectral gap and bottlenecks control each other.
long: Spectral gap and bottlenecks control each other. Conductance measures the sparsest cut relative to volume.
proof: The upper bound uses a threshold sweep of the second eigenvector; the lower bound uses a test vector from a sparse cut.
consequence: It connects expansion, mixing time, and eigenvalues.

title: Alon-Boppana Bound on Nontrivial Eigenvalues
subject: Graph Theory
statement: For any sequence of d-regular graphs, the second-largest adjacency eigenvalue satisfies liminf at least 2 times the square root of d-1.
short: Regular graphs cannot have arbitrarily small nontrivial eigenvalues.
