long: Regular graphs cannot have arbitrarily small nontrivial eigenvalues. Ramanujan graphs meet this asymptotic lower bound.
proof: Trace powers count closed walks and show eigenvalues cannot all be much smaller than the tree-like growth rate.
consequence: It defines the optimal spectral quality for expanders.

title: Ramanujan Graphs
subject: Graph Theory
statement: A d-regular graph is Ramanujan if every nontrivial adjacency eigenvalue has absolute value at most 2 times the square root of d-1.
short: Ramanujan graphs are spectrally optimal expanders.
long: Ramanujan graphs are spectrally optimal expanders. Explicit infinite families exist for suitable degrees by LPS and Marcus-Spielman-Srivastava.
proof: Constructions use Cayley graphs of groups or interlacing families of polynomials.
consequence: They are near-optimal for expansion and error-correcting codes.

title: Expander Mixing Lemma
subject: Graph Theory
statement: In a d-regular graph with second-largest eigenvalue lambda in absolute value, the edge count between sets S and T deviates from the expected value by at most lambda times the square root of their sizes.
short: Small eigenvalues force pseudorandom edge distribution.
long: Small eigenvalues force pseudorandom edge distribution. The normalized version divides the bound by n and uses d as the largest eigenvalue.
proof: Expand characteristic vectors in the eigenbasis and apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the nontrivial part.
consequence: It quantifies pseudorandomness in expanders.

title: Gershgorin Bound for Adjacency Eigenvalues
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Every adjacency eigenvalue of a graph lies in the union of disks centered at zero with radius equal to the maximum degree.
short: Row sums bound the spectral radius.
long: Row sums bound the spectral radius. For an undirected graph the disks are symmetric about zero.
proof: Apply the Gershgorin circle theorem to the symmetric adjacency matrix.
consequence: It gives a quick crude bound on graph spectra.

title: Perron Eigenvalue of a Connected Graph
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The largest adjacency eigenvalue of a connected graph is simple and has a strictly positive eigenvector.
short: Nonnegative matrices have positive top eigenvectors.
long: Nonnegative matrices have positive top eigenvectors. The eigenvalue equals the spectral radius for a connected graph.
proof: Apply the Perron-Frobenius theorem to the adjacency matrix.
consequence: It underlies PageRank and centrality measures.

title: Cospectral Nonisomorphic Graphs
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Nonisomorphic graphs can have exactly the same adjacency spectrum, so the spectrum does not determine a graph.
short: Eigenvalues do not always recover the graph.
long: Eigenvalues do not always recover the graph. The smallest such pairs already occur on six vertices.
proof: Construct two graphs with the same characteristic polynomial but different degree or subgraph structure.
consequence: It limits the power of spectral graph invariants.

title: Shannon Capacity of the Five-Cycle
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The Shannon capacity of the five-cycle equals the square root of five.
short: A graph's confusability can shrink exponentially less than expected.
long: A graph's confusability can shrink exponentially less than expected. Lovasz computed it using the theta function of the complement.
proof: The theta function gives an upper bound sqrt(5), and a two-letter code of size five gives the matching lower bound.
consequence: It showed that Shannon capacity need not be attained by a finite number of uses.

title: Lovasz Theta Sandwich Theorem
subject: Graph Theory
statement: The independence number of a graph is at most its Lovasz theta value, which is at most the chromatic number of its complement.
short: Theta sits between two classic graph parameters.
long: Theta sits between two classic graph parameters. It is computable in polynomial time by semidefinite programming.
proof: Construct feasible solutions to the primal and dual semidefinite formulations.
consequence: It gives efficient bounds on independence and chromatic number.

title: Mycielski Construction Raises Chromatic Number
subject: Graph Theory
statement: From a triangle-free k-chromatic graph, the Mycielski construction produces a triangle-free (k+1)-chromatic graph.
short: Cloned neighbours force one more colour without creating triangles.
long: Cloned neighbours force one more colour without creating triangles. It shows triangle-free graphs can have arbitrarily large chromatic number.
proof: A k-colouring of M(G) would restrict to a (k-1)-colouring of G, and no triangle is created by the construction.
consequence: It disproves the hope that clique number bounds chromatic number.

title: Hadwiger's Conjecture
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Open: every graph with chromatic number k contains a complete graph on k vertices as a minor; the claim is proved for k at most six.
short: High chromatic number should force a large clique minor.
long: High chromatic number should force a large clique minor. It generalizes the Four Colour Theorem in the case k=5.
proof: Open. The cases up to k=6 are known, but the general conjecture is unresolved.
consequence: It is one of the central open problems in structural graph theory.

title: Reconstruction Conjecture
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Open: every graph with at least three vertices is determined up to isomorphism by the multiset of its vertex-deleted subgraphs.
short: A graph's deck should identify the graph.
long: A graph's deck should identify the graph. It is known for many classes, including trees and regular graphs.
proof: Open. No proof for all graphs is known despite extensive partial results.
consequence: It asks whether local deletions encode global structure.

title: List Edge-Colouring Conjecture
subject: Graph Theory
statement: Open: the list chromatic index of every graph equals its ordinary chromatic index.
short: Edge lists should not make colouring harder.
long: Edge lists should not make colouring harder. Galvin proved the equality for bipartite multigraphs.
proof: Open. The general equality remains conjectural.
consequence: It tests how robust edge-colouring is under prescribed colour choices.

title: Axioms of Probability
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A probability measure assigns nonnegative masses to events, gives the whole space mass one, and is countably additive on disjoint events.
short: Probability is a normalized measure.
long: Probability is a normalized measure. Finite additivity follows from countable additivity by appending empty sets.
proof: These are the defining axioms of a probability measure.
consequence: All elementary probability rules derive from these axioms.

title: Complement Rule for Probabilities
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The probability of the complement of an event is one minus its probability.
short: An event and its complement partition the sample space.
long: An event and its complement partition the sample space. This is often the easiest way to compute at-least-one probabilities.
proof: Apply additivity to A and A^c and use P(Omega)=1.
consequence: It underpins many counting shortcuts.

title: Addition Rule for Two Events
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For events A and B, P(A union B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A intersection B).
short: Subtract the overlap counted twice.
long: Subtract the overlap counted twice. For disjoint events the intersection term vanishes.
proof: Decompose the union into A, B, and their overlap.
consequence: It is the basic inclusion-exclusion rule for two events.

title: Conditional Probability Definition
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For an event B with positive probability, the conditional probability of A given B is P(A intersection B) divided by P(B).
short: Restrict the sample space to B.
long: Restrict the sample space to B. It is undefined when P(B)=0.
proof: Renormalize the mass of B to total one.
consequence: It formalizes updating beliefs after observing an event.

title: Law of Total Probability
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: If events B_i partition the sample space with positive probabilities, then P(A) is the sum over i of P(A given B_i) times P(B_i).
short: Condition on each case and average.
long: Condition on each case and average. It is the discrete version of iterating expectation.
proof: Write A as the disjoint union of A intersection B_i and apply the definition of conditional probability.
consequence: It decomposes difficult probabilities into manageable cases.

title: Pairwise Independence Does Not Imply Mutual Independence
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Three events can be pairwise independent without being mutually independent.
short: Pairwise relations need not determine the triple.
long: Pairwise relations need not determine the triple. For two fair coin flips, the first head, the second head, and their XOR are pairwise independent but not jointly independent.
proof: Each pair has probability one quarter for each joint outcome, yet knowing the first two determines the third.
consequence: It warns against assuming full independence from pairwise checks.

title: Markov's Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a nonnegative random variable X and positive a, the probability that X is at least a is at most its expectation divided by a.
short: A large value cannot occur too often.
long: A large value cannot occur too often. It needs no variance assumption.
proof: Exceeding a contributes at least a times its probability to the expectation.
consequence: It is the weakest but most general concentration bound.

title: Cantelli's One-Sided Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a random variable with mean mu and variance sigma squared, the probability that X-mu is at most -a is bounded by sigma squared over sigma squared plus a squared.
short: One-sided deviations are cheaper than Chebyshev's two-sided bound.
long: One-sided deviations are cheaper than Chebyshev's two-sided bound. The analogous upper-tail bound has the same form.
proof: Apply Markov's inequality to the nonnegative quadratic (X-mu+t)^2 and optimize over t.
consequence: It improves Chebyshev when only one tail matters.

title: Chernoff Bound for Bernoulli Sums
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a sum S of independent Bernoulli variables with mean mu, the probability that S is at least (1+delta)mu is at most exp(-delta^2 mu/(2+delta)).
short: Exponential tails follow from moment generating functions.
long: Exponential tails follow from moment generating functions. A matching lower-tail bound has exponent -mu delta^2/2.
proof: Bound E exp(lambda S), apply Markov's inequality, and optimize over lambda.
consequence: It is the standard tail bound for counts and sampling.

title: Hoeffding's Inequality for Bounded Variables
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For independent bounded variables, the deviation of their sum from its mean has a sub-Gaussian tail depending on the sum of squared ranges.
short: Bounded independent noise is sub-Gaussian.
long: Bounded independent noise is sub-Gaussian. It applies to sums of bounded functions and empirical means.
proof: Hoeffding's lemma bounds each centered mgf by a Gaussian mgf, then Markov's inequality is optimized.
consequence: It is a clean tool for finite-sample concentration.

title: Azuma's Inequality for Bounded Martingale Differences
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A martingale whose differences are bounded by c_i has tail probability at most twice the exponential of minus t squared over twice the sum of c_i squared.
short: Martingales with small steps concentrate.
long: Martingales with small steps concentrate. It is the martingale analogue of Hoeffding's inequality.
proof: Apply Hoeffding's lemma conditionally to each martingale difference and iterate.
consequence: It proves concentration for sequential and randomized algorithms.

title: McDiarmid's Bounded Differences Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A function of independent variables with each coordinate change affecting it by at most c_i concentrates around its expectation with a sub-Gaussian tail.
short: Low sensitivity to any one input yields concentration.
long: Low sensitivity to any one input yields concentration. It applies to combinatorial quantities such as coloring counts and matching sizes.
proof: Form the Doob martingale revealing variables one at a time and apply Azuma's inequality.
consequence: It extends concentration from sums to general functions.

title: Berry-Esseen Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For i.i.d. centred variables with finite third absolute moment, the Kolmogorov distance to the normal limit is bounded by a constant times the standardized third moment divided by the square root of n.
short: It quantifies the speed of the central limit theorem.
long: It quantifies the speed of the central limit theorem. The constant is universal but not needed for most applications.
proof: Use characteristic functions and smoothing inequalities to control the approximation error.
consequence: It turns the CLT from a qualitative into a quantitative result.

title: Lindeberg Central Limit Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A triangular array of independent variables with finite variances converges to a normal law when the Lindeberg condition holds.
short: No single variable may dominate the sum.
long: No single variable may dominate the sum. It generalizes the classical i.i.d. central limit theorem.
proof: Compare characteristic functions with the Gaussian expansion under the Lindeberg condition.
consequence: It handles non-identically distributed summands.

title: Slutsky's Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: If X_n converges in distribution to X and Y_n converges in probability to a constant c, then X_n+Y_n converges in distribution to X+c.
short: A vanishing random perturbation does not change a weak limit.
long: A vanishing random perturbation does not change a weak limit. Products and ratios have analogous versions when the limit constant is nonzero for division.
proof: Use the continuous mapping theorem and convergence in probability of the pair.
consequence: It is used constantly in asymptotic statistics.

title: Continuous Mapping Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: If X_n converges in distribution to X and g is continuous on the support of X, then g(X_n) converges in distribution to g(X).
short: Continuous functions preserve weak convergence.
long: Continuous functions preserve weak convergence. Measurability and continuity at the limit points are the key hypotheses.
proof: Apply the portmanteau theorem to closed sets and their preimages.
consequence: It justifies the delta method and many transformations.

title: Delta Method for Asymptotic Variance
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: If the scaled estimation error converges to a normal law and g is differentiable, then the scaled error of g of the estimator converges to a normal law with variance scaled by the derivative squared.
short: A smooth transformation inherits asymptotic normality.
long: A smooth transformation inherits asymptotic normality. The first-order Taylor expansion dominates the error.
proof: Apply the continuous mapping theorem to the linear approximation from Taylor's theorem.
consequence: It provides standard errors for transformed estimates.

title: Cramer's Large Deviation Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The sample mean of i.i.d. random variables satisfies a large deviation principle whose rate function is the Legendre transform of the log moment generating function.
short: Rare deviations decay at an exponential rate given by entropy-like geometry.
long: Rare deviations decay at an exponential rate given by entropy-like geometry. It requires the moment generating function to be finite in a neighbourhood of the optimizing parameter.
proof: The Gartner-Ellis theorem yields the lower and upper large deviation bounds.
consequence: It quantifies probabilities far from the typical value.

title: Sanov's Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The empirical distribution of i.i.d. samples satisfies a large deviation principle with rate equal to Kullback-Leibler divergence from the true distribution.
short: Atypical empirical measures are penalized by relative entropy.
long: Atypical empirical measures are penalized by relative entropy. The method of types makes the result particularly transparent for finite alphabets.
proof: Count typical sequences of each type and apply Stirling's formula.
consequence: It links information theory and large deviations.

title: Jensen's Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a convex function phi, the value at the expectation is at most the expectation of the value.
short: Convexity pushes averages upward.
long: Convexity pushes averages upward. For concave functions the inequality reverses.
proof: Use a supporting line at the mean and take expectations.
consequence: It underlies entropy bounds and many moment inequalities.

title: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality in Expectation Form
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The squared expectation of a product is at most the product of the second moments.
short: Correlation is bounded by one.
long: Correlation is bounded by one. It is equivalent to nonnegativity of the variance of a linear combination.
proof: The quadratic polynomial in t given by E(X-tY)^2 is nonnegative, so its discriminant is at most zero.
consequence: It is the workhorse of probability and statistics.

title: Paley-Zygmund Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a nonnegative random variable and any theta between zero and one, the probability that X exceeds theta times its mean is at least (1-theta)^2 times the squared mean over the second moment.
short: A lower tail bound complements Markov's upper tail.
long: A lower tail bound complements Markov's upper tail. It is useful when a random quantity has small second moment relative to its mean.
proof: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the indicator of the event and the square root of X.
consequence: It gives existence proofs by showing positive probability.

title: Kolmogorov's Maximal Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For partial sums of independent centred variables, the probability that the maximum absolute partial sum reaches t is at most the final variance divided by t squared.
short: A maximum of a martingale is controlled by its final variance.
long: A maximum of a martingale is controlled by its final variance. It strengthens Chebyshev from one time to the whole path.
proof: Apply the optional stopping idea at the first hitting time and use orthogonality of martingale increments.
consequence: It proves strong laws and martingale convergence results.

title: Doob's Martingale Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a nonnegative submartingale, lambda times the probability that its maximum reaches lambda is at most the expectation of the terminal value on that event.
short: The maximum of a submartingale is integrable.
long: The maximum of a submartingale is integrable. The L^p version controls the p-th moment of the maximum by the p-th moment of the terminal value.
proof: Decompose by the first crossing time and use the submartingale property.
consequence: It is essential for convergence proofs and maximal functions.

title: Martingale Convergence Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A martingale bounded in L^2 converges almost surely and in L^2 to a limit.
short: Bounded martingales settle down.
long: Bounded martingales settle down. The L^1 version requires uniform integrability for convergence in mean.
proof: Upcrossing inequalities show almost sure convergence; L^2 boundedness gives convergence in norm.
consequence: It underpins likelihood ratio martingales and conditional expectation limits.

title: Strong Markov Property
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A stochastic process with the Markov property also resets after any almost surely finite stopping time.
short: The future depends on the stopping-time state only.
long: The future depends on the stopping-time state only. It is crucial for hitting-time and excursion analyses.
proof: Approximate the stopping time by countably valued stopping times and apply the ordinary Markov property.
consequence: It underlies Brownian motion and Markov chain hitting computations.

title: Stationary Distribution of a Markov Chain
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A probability vector is stationary for a transition matrix if multiplying the matrix leaves it unchanged; irreducible positive recurrent chains have a unique one.
short: Stationarity means the distribution does not drift.
long: Stationarity means the distribution does not drift. A finite irreducible chain is always positive recurrent.
proof: Existence follows from Perron-Frobenius; uniqueness from irreducibility.
consequence: It identifies the long-run distribution of a chain.

title: Detailed Balance Condition
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A distribution and transition matrix satisfy detailed balance when the flow from i to j equals the flow from j to i for every pair.
short: Reversibility makes stationarity obvious.
long: Reversibility makes stationarity obvious. Detailed balance is sufficient but not necessary for stationarity.
proof: Summing the condition over i shows the j-th entry of pi P equals pi_j.
consequence: It is the design principle behind MCMC algorithms.

title: Convergence of Finite Aperiodic Markov Chains
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A finite irreducible aperiodic Markov chain converges to its unique stationary distribution from any starting state.
short: Mixing removes the memory of the initial state.
long: Mixing removes the memory of the initial state. Aperiodicity rules out periodic oscillation.
proof: Perron-Frobenius gives all other eigenvalues modulus strictly less than one.
consequence: It justifies long-run simulation and MCMC.

title: Mixing and Cover Time of Random Walk on a Complete Graph
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A random walk on the complete graph on n vertices mixes in order log n steps and covers all vertices in order n log n steps.
short: Coupon collecting dominates the cover time.
long: Coupon collecting dominates the cover time. The spectral gap is of order one over n.
proof: The transition matrix has second eigenvalue -1/(n-1), and coupon-collector analysis gives the cover time.
consequence: It is the simplest benchmark for mixing-time calculations.

title: Poisson Limit of Binomial Counts
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Binomial(n,lambda/n) distributions converge to the Poisson distribution with mean lambda as n tends to infinity.
short: Rare independent events with stable mean give Poisson counts.
long: Rare independent events with stable mean give Poisson counts. This is the law of rare events.
proof: Take the limit of the binomial probability generating function.
consequence: It justifies Poisson approximations in queueing and reliability.

title: Thinning a Poisson Process
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Keeping each point of a rate lambda Poisson process independently with probability p yields a rate lambda p Poisson process.
short: Independent thinning preserves the Poisson structure.
long: Independent thinning preserves the Poisson structure. The kept and discarded processes are independent.
proof: Independent increments and Poisson counts in intervals transfer to the thinned counts.
consequence: It models competing risks and filtered arrivals.

title: Memorylessness of the Exponential Distribution
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For an exponential waiting time, conditioning on survival past s leaves the remaining time exponentially distributed with the same rate.
short: The distribution forgets how long it has already waited.
long: The distribution forgets how long it has already waited. It is the unique continuous distribution with this property.
proof: Divide the survival function exp(-lambda(s+t)) by exp(-lambda s).
consequence: It makes the exponential natural for Poisson process interarrival times.

title: Gamma Distribution as a Sum of Exponentials
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The sum of k independent exponential variables with rate lambda has a gamma distribution with shape k and rate lambda.
short: Waiting for the k-th arrival sums k waiting times.
long: Waiting for the k-th arrival sums k waiting times. For integer shape the gamma is also called Erlang.
proof: Convolution or moment generating functions multiply the Laplace transforms.
consequence: It connects Poisson processes and gamma waiting times.

title: Uniform Order Statistics Are Beta Distributed
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The k-th order statistic of n independent uniform variables on the unit interval has a beta distribution with parameters k and n-k+1.
short: The k-th order statistic balances k below and n-k+1 above.
long: The k-th order statistic balances k below and n-k+1 above. Its mean is k over n+1.
proof: Differentiate the binomial probability that at least k samples are at most x.
consequence: It underpins nonparametric quantile inference.

title: Beta-Binomial Conjugacy
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A beta prior updated by binomial data remains beta, and the predictive distribution of successes is beta-binomial.
short: Beta parameters behave like pseudo-counts.
long: Beta parameters behave like pseudo-counts. The posterior mean is a weighted average of prior mean and sample proportion.
proof: Multiply the beta density by the binomial likelihood and match exponents.
consequence: It is a canonical example of conjugate Bayesian updating.

title: Normal-Normal Conjugacy
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A normal prior for a normal mean with known variance yields a normal posterior, with precision equal to prior precision plus data precision.
short: Precisions add in Gaussian updating.
long: Precisions add in Gaussian updating. The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of prior mean and sample mean.
proof: Complete the square in the exponent of prior times likelihood.
consequence: It illustrates shrinkage and the role of precision.

title: Conditional Multivariate Normal Distribution
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A subvector of a multivariate normal vector conditioned on another subvector is again multivariate normal, with covariance given by a Schur complement.
short: Gaussian conditionals stay Gaussian.
long: Gaussian conditionals stay Gaussian. The conditional mean is linear in the conditioning value.
proof: Complete the square in the joint density or use characteristic functions.
consequence: It is fundamental for Gaussian networks and Kalman filtering.

title: Covariance Matrices Are Positive Semidefinite
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For any random vector, its covariance matrix is positive semidefinite.
short: Every variance is nonnegative.
long: Every variance is nonnegative. Positive definiteness requires the distribution not to be supported on a proper affine subspace.
proof: Apply the definition of covariance to a linear combination of the coordinates.
consequence: It constrains valid correlation structures.

title: Correlation Does Not Imply Causation
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Two variables can be strongly correlated without either causing the other, for example because both respond to a hidden common cause.
short: Association alone has no direction.
long: Association alone has no direction. Confounding, selection effects, and reverse causation all produce correlation.
proof: Construct X and Y as independent functions of a common latent variable Z.
consequence: Causal claims require design or assumptions beyond statistics.

title: Simpson's Paradox
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: An association that holds in every subgroup can reverse when the groups are pooled.
short: Different group sizes can reverse the aggregate trend.
long: Different group sizes can reverse the aggregate trend. It arises when a lurking variable affects both the grouping and the outcome.
proof: Construct two groups with different baselines and unequal sample allocations, then compare weighted averages.
consequence: It warns against drawing conclusions from aggregated data.

title: Berkson's Paradox
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Conditioning on a common effect can create a negative association between two independent causes.
short: Selection on a collider induces dependence.
long: Selection on a collider induces dependence. It is also called collider bias in causal inference.
proof: Condition on an event that requires at least one of two independent causes, making the other less likely.
consequence: It explains spurious associations in selected samples.

title: Kolmogorov's Zero-One Law
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Any tail event of a sequence of independent random variables has probability either zero or one.
short: Events independent of every finite initial segment are deterministic.
long: Events independent of every finite initial segment are deterministic. Examples include convergence of a series of independent variables.
proof: Approximate the tail event by events depending on finitely many variables and apply independence.
consequence: It decides many limiting questions as deterministic.

title: Hewitt-Savage Zero-One Law
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Any event invariant under all finite permutations of an i.i.d. sequence has probability zero or one.
short: Symmetric events for i.i.d. sequences are deterministic.
long: Symmetric events for i.i.d. sequences are deterministic. It uses the reversed martingale of permutation-invariant sigma-algebras.
proof: Show the invariant sigma-algebra is trivial by averaging over permutations.
consequence: It generalizes the Kolmogorov zero-one law for i.i.d. sequences.

title: Law of the Iterated Logarithm
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For i.i.d. centred variables with variance one, the limsup of the partial sum divided by the square root of two n log log n is almost surely one.
short: It gives the exact boundary of the fluctuations in the law of large numbers.
long: It gives the exact boundary of the fluctuations in the law of large numbers. The liminf is minus one under the same conditions.
proof: Kolmogorov's upper and lower class arguments give the two inequalities.
consequence: It refines both the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem.

title: Glivenko-Cantelli Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The empirical distribution function converges uniformly to the true distribution function almost surely.
short: The empirical CDF learns the whole distribution.
long: The empirical CDF learns the whole distribution. Uniform convergence is much stronger than pointwise convergence at each fixed x.
proof: Use the Vapnik-Chervonenkis inequality or a uniform law of large numbers for half-lines.
consequence: It justifies the empirical CDF as a nonparametric estimator.

title: Definition of Brownian Motion
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A standard Brownian motion is a continuous Gaussian process with independent increments and variance of an increment equal to its time length.
short: It is the continuous limit of a random walk.
long: It is the continuous limit of a random walk. It has continuous but almost surely nowhere differentiable paths.
proof: Existence follows from the Kolmogorov extension theorem and continuity estimates.
consequence: It models diffusion, financial noise, and thermal fluctuations.

title: Reflection Principle for Brownian Motion
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For standard Brownian motion, the probability that the maximum up to time t reaches level a is twice the probability that the terminal value exceeds a.
short: Reflect paths after their first hit of the level.
long: Reflect paths after their first hit of the level. It also gives the distribution of the first hitting time.
proof: Paths that hit a and end below a pair with paths that end above a by reflection after the hitting time.
consequence: It yields explicit hitting-time and maximum distributions.

title: Shannon Entropy Definition
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The entropy of a discrete random variable is minus the sum over outcomes of probability times its logarithm, usually base two.
short: Entropy measures average surprise.
long: Entropy measures average surprise. A deterministic variable has entropy zero and a uniform variable on m outcomes has entropy log base two of m.
proof: The definition follows from the axioms of additive uncertainty.
consequence: It quantifies information and compressibility.

title: Chain Rule for Entropy
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The joint entropy of two variables equals the entropy of one plus the conditional entropy of the other.
short: Uncertainty splits into marginal and remaining uncertainty.
long: Uncertainty splits into marginal and remaining uncertainty. Repeated application gives entropy of a sequence as a sum of conditional entropies.
proof: Take logarithms of the joint probability factorization and average.
consequence: It drives information-theoretic identities and coding arguments.

title: Mutual Information of Random Variables
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The mutual information of two variables is the reduction in entropy of one after observing the other.
short: It measures shared information.
long: It measures shared information. It equals the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals.
proof: Rewrite the definition using the logarithm of the joint-to-product ratio.
consequence: It is central to communication and feature selection.

title: Data Processing Inequality
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For a Markov chain X to Y to Z, the mutual information between X and Z is at most that between X and Y.
short: Processing cannot create information about the original source.
long: Processing cannot create information about the original source. Equality holds when the intermediate variable is a sufficient statistic.
proof: Use convexity of relative entropy and the Markov factorization.
consequence: It bounds what any downstream transformation can preserve.

title: Gibbs Inequality for Relative Entropy
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The Kullback-Leibler divergence between two probability distributions is nonnegative and is zero exactly when they agree.
short: A logger always beats an average log ratio.
long: A logger always beats an average log ratio. It is also called information inequality or Gibbs' inequality.
proof: Apply Jensen's inequality to the convex function -log under p.
consequence: It underlies maximum likelihood and hypothesis testing.

title: Asymptotic Equipartition Property
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For an i.i.d. source, the negative log probability per symbol of a typical sequence converges in probability to the entropy rate.
short: Long samples look like roughly equiprobable typical sequences.
long: Long samples look like roughly equiprobable typical sequences. The typical set has probability near one and size about 2 to the nH.
proof: Apply the law of large numbers to the independent information values of symbols.
consequence: It is the core of Shannon's source coding theorem.

title: Maximum Entropy Distributions
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Subject to fixed mean and variance on the real line, the Gaussian maximizes entropy; subject to a fixed mean on the nonnegative reals, the exponential does.
short: Least-informative distributions have familiar forms.
long: Least-informative distributions have familiar forms. The constraints are enforced with Lagrange multipliers.
proof: Variational calculus gives a density exponential in the constraint functions.
consequence: It justifies Gaussian and exponential assumptions under minimal knowledge.

title: Variance of the Sample Mean
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: For independent identically distributed variables with variance sigma squared, the sample mean has variance sigma squared divided by n.
short: Averaging independent noise reduces variance.
long: Averaging independent noise reduces variance. The standard error therefore shrinks like one over the square root of n.
proof: Compute the variance of a sum using independence and divide by n squared.
consequence: It explains the precision gain from larger samples.

title: Unbiasedness of the Sample Variance
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Dividing the sum of squared deviations by n-1 yields an unbiased estimator of the population variance.
short: One degree of freedom is lost by estimating the mean.
long: One degree of freedom is lost by estimating the mean. Dividing by n instead gives a downward-biased estimator.
proof: Expand the identity sum (X_i-bar X)^2 = sum (X_i-mu)^2 - n(bar X-mu)^2 and take expectations.
consequence: Bessel's correction is standard in variance estimation.

title: Cramer-Rao Lower Bound
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Under regularity conditions, the variance of any unbiased estimator of a parameter is at least the reciprocal of the Fisher information.
short: Information sets a floor on estimator precision.
long: Information sets a floor on estimator precision. Equality characterizes efficient estimators in regular families.
proof: Apply Cauchy-Schwarz to the score function and the estimator's derivative in expectation.
consequence: It benchmarks estimator efficiency.

title: Rao-Blackwell Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Conditioning any estimator on a sufficient statistic does not increase its expected squared error.
short: Sufficient statistics discard noise.
long: Sufficient statistics discard noise. The improvement follows by Jensen's inequality for the squared loss.
proof: Use the tower property and convexity of squared error under conditional expectation.
consequence: It motivates searching for sufficient statistics.

title: Fisher Information Definition
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Fisher information is the expected squared derivative of the log likelihood, equivalently minus the expected second derivative under regularity conditions.
short: It measures how sharply data identify a parameter.
long: It measures how sharply data identify a parameter. Information from independent observations adds.
proof: Differentiate the likelihood identity and use the score's mean zero.
consequence: It appears in asymptotic efficiency and the Cramer-Rao bound.

title: Neyman-Pearson Lemma
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Among tests with a fixed type I error for two simple hypotheses, the likelihood-ratio test has the greatest power.
short: Reject when the likelihood ratio is large.
long: Reject when the likelihood ratio is large. Randomization may be needed to hit an exact size.
proof: Optimize the integral of the test function under the alternative subject to the size constraint.
consequence: It is the foundation of optimal hypothesis testing.

title: Definition of a p-Value
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A p-value is the probability, under the null hypothesis, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.
short: It measures compatibility of data with the null.
long: It measures compatibility of data with the null. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
proof: It is computed from the null distribution of the chosen statistic.
consequence: It is the most common, and most misused, statistical summary.

title: Type I and Type II Errors
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: A type I error rejects a true null hypothesis; a type II error fails to reject a false null, and power is one minus the type II error probability.
short: False positives and false negatives trade off.
long: False positives and false negatives trade off. Fixing the significance level controls alpha but says nothing directly about beta.
proof: These are definitions based on the two possible states of nature and decisions.
consequence: Sample-size planning is usually framed in terms of these errors.
wiki: Type I and type II errors

title: Bonferroni Correction
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Testing m hypotheses each at level alpha divided by m controls the family-wise error rate at most alpha.
short: Union bound keeps the chance of any false positive small.
long: Union bound keeps the chance of any false positive small. It is conservative when tests are positively dependent.
proof: The probability of at least one false rejection is at most the sum of the individual probabilities.
consequence: It is the simplest multiple-testing correction.

title: Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The step-up procedure that rejects the smallest p-values up to the largest satisfying p_(i) <= i alpha/m controls the false discovery rate under independence.
short: FDR control is less conservative than family-wise control.
long: FDR control is less conservative than family-wise control. It allows a controlled fraction of false discoveries among rejections.
proof: Bound the expected ratio of false rejections to total rejections using independence of p-values.
consequence: It is standard in large-scale testing.

title: Bootstrap Resampling
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Drawing samples with replacement from the observed data approximates the sampling distribution of a statistic.
short: Let the empirical distribution stand in for the true one.
long: Let the empirical distribution stand in for the true one. The bootstrap is consistent for many smooth statistics.
proof: Conditional on the data, bootstrap samples are i.i.d. from the empirical distribution, which converges to the truth.
consequence: It estimates standard errors and intervals without analytic derivation.

title: Bias-Variance Decomposition
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Expected squared prediction error splits into squared bias, variance, and irreducible noise.
short: Model error has three distinct sources.
long: Model error has three distinct sources. More flexible models usually lower bias but raise variance.
proof: Add and subtract the mean of the fitted model, then expand the square.
consequence: It explains overfitting and the need for regularization.

title: Gauss-Markov Theorem
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Under linearity, zero mean errors, homoscedasticity, and uncorrelated errors, ordinary least squares is the best linear unbiased estimator.
short: OLS is optimal among linear unbiased estimators.
long: OLS is optimal among linear unbiased estimators. It does not require normally distributed errors.
proof: Write any linear unbiased estimator as OLS plus an orthogonal term and compare variances.
consequence: It justifies least squares in the classical linear model.

title: Least Squares Normal Equations
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: The least-squares coefficient vector satisfies the normal equations obtained by setting the gradient of the residual sum of squares to zero.
short: Residuals are orthogonal to the regressors.
long: Residuals are orthogonal to the regressors. The solution is unique when the design matrix has full column rank.
proof: Differentiate the quadratic objective and equate to zero.
consequence: It is the computational basis of linear regression.

title: EM Algorithm Monotonicity
subject: Probability & Statistics
statement: Each expectation-maximization step never decreases the observed-data likelihood.
short: Maximize a lower bound on the likelihood.
long: Maximize a lower bound on the likelihood. It is widely used with latent variables and missing data.
proof: Jensen's inequality gives a surrogate objective touched at the current parameter; maximizing it improves the true likelihood.
consequence: It provides stable iterative estimation for mixtures and hidden models.

title: Definition of a Smooth Manifold
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: A smooth manifold is a Hausdorff second-countable space locally homeomorphic to Euclidean space with smoothly compatible charts.
short: It is a space that looks like Euclidean space up close.
long: It is a space that looks like Euclidean space up close. Compatibility means chart changes are smooth maps.
proof: The definition supplies the local coordinate structure needed for calculus.
consequence: It provides the setting for differential geometry.

title: Tangent Space of a Manifold
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The tangent space at a point is the vector space of derivations of germs of smooth functions, equivalently equivalence classes of curves with the same velocity.
short: It collects possible velocities at a point.
long: It collects possible velocities at a point. Its dual is the cotangent space of covectors.
proof: In a chart, derivations are identified with partial derivative operators.
consequence: It lets one do linear algebra pointwise on curved spaces.

title: Differential Forms
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: A differential k-form is a smooth antisymmetric covariant k-tensor field on a manifold.
short: Forms are integrands over oriented submanifolds.
long: Forms are integrands over oriented submanifolds. They form a graded algebra under the wedge product.
proof: Local coordinate expressions transform by the Jacobian determinant under chart changes.
consequence: They unify line integrals, surface integrals, and Stokes' theorem.

title: Exterior Derivative and Its Square
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The exterior derivative maps k-forms to (k+1)-forms and satisfies d composed with d equals zero.
short: Boundaries have no boundary.
long: Boundaries have no boundary. On functions it recovers the ordinary differential.
proof: Check in coordinates using symmetry of second partial derivatives.
consequence: The identity d squared zero defines de Rham cohomology.

title: Generalized Stokes' Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The integral of the exterior derivative of a compactly supported form over an oriented manifold equals the integral of the form over its boundary.
short: It unifies the fundamental theorem of calculus with Green and Gauss theorems.
long: It unifies the fundamental theorem of calculus with Green and Gauss theorems. Sign conventions depend on boundary orientation.
proof: Reduce to Euclidean half-space using a partition of unity and apply the fundamental theorem of calculus.
consequence: It is the central integration theorem on manifolds.

title: de Rham Cohomology
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The k-th de Rham cohomology group is the space of closed k-forms modulo exact k-forms.
short: It measures closed forms that are not boundaries.
long: It measures closed forms that are not boundaries. It is a homotopy invariant of the manifold.
proof: The identity d squared zero makes closed forms a chain complex.
consequence: It connects analysis with topology.

title: Poincare Lemma
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: On a contractible open set such as a star-shaped domain, every closed differential form is exact.
short: Locally, closed forms always have potentials.
long: Locally, closed forms always have potentials. Global topology can obstruct exactness.
proof: Construct a homotopy operator from the contraction to a point.
consequence: It shows de Rham cohomology is a global, not local, invariant.

title: Homotopy of Continuous Maps
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Two continuous maps are homotopic if one can be continuously deformed into the other through a family of maps.
short: Homotopy is continuous deformation.
long: Homotopy is continuous deformation. Homotopic maps induce the same maps on homotopy and homology groups.
proof: The prism operator in singular homology gives a chain homotopy between induced maps.
consequence: It defines the basic equivalence in algebraic topology.

title: Fundamental Group
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The fundamental group consists of homotopy classes of loops based at a point, with concatenation as the group operation.
short: It records how loops can be deformed.
long: It records how loops can be deformed. Changing basepoint in a path-connected space gives isomorphic groups.
proof: Associativity holds up to homotopy and inverses are traversed backwards.
consequence: It detects holes and covering spaces.

title: Lifting Theorem for Covering Spaces
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: A map from a simply connected, locally path-connected space to a covering space lifts uniquely once the image of the basepoint is chosen.
short: Simple connectivity removes monodromy.
long: Simple connectivity removes monodromy. It underlies the classification of covering spaces by subgroups of the fundamental group.
proof: Lift locally and continue uniquely along paths; simple connectivity makes the result path-independent.
consequence: It connects covering theory with group subgroups.

title: Seifert-van Kampen Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The fundamental group of a space covered by two path-connected open sets with path-connected intersection is the amalgamated free product of the fundamental groups of the pieces.
short: Compute a big fundamental group from smaller ones.
long: Compute a big fundamental group from smaller ones. It is the main computational tool for fundamental groups.
proof: Represent loops by words in loops of the two pieces and impose relations from the intersection.
consequence: It makes many fundamental groups computable.

title: Singular Homology Groups
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Singular homology groups are obtained from chain groups of continuous simplices and boundary maps whose square is zero.
short: They count holes of each dimension algebraically.
long: They count holes of each dimension algebraically. Homology is functorial for continuous maps and homotopy invariant.
proof: The boundary of a boundary is zero, so the quotient by boundaries is well-defined.
consequence: It provides computable topological invariants.

title: Euler Characteristic via Betti Numbers
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: For a finite CW complex, the Euler characteristic equals the alternating sum of its Betti numbers.
short: Cells and homology ranks give the same alternating count.
long: Cells and homology ranks give the same alternating count. It holds with any coefficient field of characteristic zero.
proof: Alternate the rank-nullity equations for the cellular chain complex.
consequence: It connects combinatorial cell counts with homology.

title: Brouwer Degree
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The degree of a map between closed oriented manifolds of the same dimension is the integer measuring how many times it wraps the domain around the target.
short: Degree counts oriented preimages.
long: Degree counts oriented preimages. It is a homotopy invariant and generalizes winding number.
proof: Count preimages of a regular value with signs, or use induced maps on top homology.
consequence: It gives fixed-point and existence theorems.

title: Lefschetz Fixed-Point Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: If the Lefschetz number of a self-map of a suitable finite complex is nonzero, then the map has a fixed point.
short: Homology can force fixed points.
long: Homology can force fixed points. It generalizes Brouwer's fixed-point theorem.
proof: If there were no fixed points, the Lefschetz number vanishes by the Lefschetz-Hopf trace formula.
consequence: It converts algebraic data into existence of fixed points.

title: CW Complexes
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: A CW complex is built by attaching cells of increasing dimension along maps from their boundaries into the previously constructed skeleton.
short: Spaces can be assembled one cell at a time.
long: Spaces can be assembled one cell at a time. The weak topology requires a set to be closed when its intersection with every cell closure is closed.
proof: The construction recursively defines the skeleta and attaching maps.
consequence: CW complexes are the natural spaces for algebraic topology.

title: Homology of the n-Sphere
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: For n at least one, the reduced homology of the n-sphere is nontrivial only in degree n, where it is the integers.
short: A sphere has one hole in its own dimension.
long: A sphere has one hole in its own dimension. Reduced homology is zero in all other degrees.
proof: Use Mayer-Vietoris with two overlapping hemispheres and induction on dimension.
consequence: It is the basic benchmark computation in homology.

title: Homology of the Two-Torus
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The torus has first homology equal to the integer lattice of rank two and second homology equal to the integers.
short: Two loops and one surface class.
long: Two loops and one surface class. The rank of first homology matches two independent directions around the torus.
proof: Use the product decomposition as a circle times a circle and the Kunnetheorem.
consequence: It illustrates homology of product spaces.

title: Fundamental Group of the Circle
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The fundamental group of the circle is isomorphic to the integers, with isomorphism given by winding number.
short: Loops are classified by how many times they wind.
long: Loops are classified by how many times they wind. The universal cover is the real line mapping by the exponential.
proof: Unique lifting to the real line assigns an integer endpoint change.
consequence: It is the simplest example of a nontrivial fundamental group.

title: Fundamental Group of the Torus
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The fundamental group of the two-dimensional torus is the free abelian group on two generators.
short: Loops commuting around two directions give a lattice.
long: Loops commuting around two directions give a lattice. It is abelian, unlike the fundamental group of a wedge of two circles.
proof: Use the product property pi_1(X times Y) is the product of pi_1 of the factors.
consequence: It distinguishes the torus from surfaces with nonabelian fundamental group.

title: Fundamental Group of the Figure Eight
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The fundamental group of a wedge of two circles is the free group on two generators.
short: Loops form freely reduced words in two letters.
long: Loops form freely reduced words in two letters. There are no relations beyond cancellation of inverse letters.
proof: Apply Seifert-van Kampen to two circle neighbourhoods with contractible intersection.
consequence: It is the canonical example of a nonabelian fundamental group.

title: Orientability of Manifolds
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: A manifold is orientable when it admits a consistent choice of orientation across overlapping charts.
short: One can choose a global notion of counterclockwise.
long: One can choose a global notion of counterclockwise. Equivalently, the top Stiefel-Whitney class vanishes.
proof: Check that orientation signs of chart changes can all be made positive.
consequence: Orientability is required for integration of top-degree forms.

title: Knots as Embedded Circles
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: A knot is a smooth embedding of a circle in three-dimensional space, considered up to ambient isotopy.
short: A knot is a tangled loop that cannot pass through itself.
long: A knot is a tangled loop that cannot pass through itself. Equivalence means a continuous deformation of the surrounding space.
proof: The definition specifies the objects and the isotopy relation.
consequence: Knot theory studies embeddings rather than intrinsic topology of the circle.

title: Reidemeister Moves for Knot Diagrams
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Two knot diagrams represent the same knot if and only if they are related by a sequence of Reidemeister moves and planar isotopy.
short: Three local moves capture all knot equivalence.
long: Three local moves capture all knot equivalence. They modify a diagram without changing the underlying knot.
proof: Isotopy can be approximated by a sequence of these local picture changes.
consequence: Knot invariants can be checked on diagrams via these moves.

title: Trefoil Is Not the Unknot
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The trefoil knot cannot be deformed to an unknotted circle; its Alexander polynomial is nontrivial.
short: A knot invariant detects the tangle.
long: A knot invariant detects the tangle. A planar diagram with three crossings captures the simplest nontrivial knot.
proof: The Alexander polynomial of the unknot is one, while the trefoil's is not.
consequence: It shows diagrams alone can be misleading without invariants.

title: Alexander Polynomial of a Knot
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The Alexander polynomial is a knot invariant derived from the infinite cyclic cover of the knot complement, normalized up to multiplication by a unit.
short: It is a polynomial invariant of a knot.
long: It is a polynomial invariant of a knot. It satisfies a skein relation relating crossing changes.
proof: Compute the homology of the cyclic cover as a module over the Laurent polynomial ring.
consequence: It was the first widely used knot polynomial.

title: Jones Polynomial of a Knot
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The Jones polynomial is a Laurent polynomial knot invariant satisfying a skein relation for over and under crossings.
short: It distinguishes knots via a recursive crossing rule.
long: It distinguishes knots via a recursive crossing rule. It can be defined through the Kauffman bracket and writhe.
proof: Show the bracket is invariant under Reidemeister moves after normalization.
consequence: It opened modern quantum topology.

title: Borromean Rings Have Zero Pairwise Linking
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Any two components of the Borromean rings have linking number zero, yet the three-component link cannot be separated.
short: The linkage is a genuinely triple interaction.
long: The linkage is a genuinely triple interaction. It is detected by a Milnor triple linking invariant.
proof: Pairwise linking numbers vanish, but a higher-order invariant is nonzero.
consequence: It shows pairwise invariants do not determine a link.

title: Theorema Egregium
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Gaussian curvature of a surface is intrinsic: it is determined by distances measured within the surface alone.
short: Bending without stretching cannot change Gaussian curvature.
long: Bending without stretching cannot change Gaussian curvature. Gauss derived an expression for K using only the first fundamental form.
proof: The Brioschi formula expresses K through first fundamental form coefficients and their derivatives.
consequence: It marks the birth of intrinsic differential geometry.

title: Bonnet-Myers Diameter Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: A complete Riemannian manifold with Ricci curvature at least (n-1)k positive has diameter at most pi divided by the square root of k.
short: Positive Ricci curvature bounds the size of the manifold.
long: Positive Ricci curvature bounds the size of the manifold. It also implies compactness and finiteness of the fundamental group.
proof: The second variation formula shows geodesics longer than that bound cannot minimize.
consequence: It is a foundational curvature comparison theorem.

title: Brunn-Minkowski Inequality
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: For nonempty compact sets in Euclidean space, the n-th root of the volume of their Minkowski sum is at least the sum of their volume roots.
short: Adding sets expands volume at least additively in root-volume.
long: Adding sets expands volume at least additively in root-volume. It implies the isoperimetric inequality and many convexity results.
proof: Prove by induction on dimension using slicing and the one-dimensional Brunn-Minkowski inequality.
consequence: It is a central inequality in convex geometry.

title: Caratheodory's Convex Hull Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Every point in the convex hull of a set in R^d lies in the convex hull of at most d+1 of its points.
short: No more than d+1 points are needed.
long: No more than d+1 points are needed. It bounds the complexity of convex combinations.
proof: Take a representation of minimal length; if more than d+1 points occur they are affinely dependent, allowing a shorter one.
consequence: It underlies Helly's theorem and computational geometry.

title: Helly's Theorem in Euclidean Space
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: For a finite family of convex sets in R^d, if every d+1 of them intersect then the whole family intersects.
short: Local intersection implies global intersection.
long: Local intersection implies global intersection. The bound d+1 is sharp.
proof: Induct on dimension using Radon's theorem to reduce a minimal non-intersecting family.
consequence: It has many applications to convex optimization and combinatorial geometry.

title: Kepler Conjecture on Sphere Packing
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: The densest packing of congruent spheres in three-dimensional space has density pi divided by three times the square root of two.
short: The familiar pyramid stacking is optimal.
long: The familiar pyramid stacking is optimal. It was proved by Hales with a large computer-assisted verification.
proof: Reduce to a finite optimization over local configurations and verify by interval arithmetic.
consequence: It settled a centuries-old question about packing.

title: Tverberg's Theorem
subject: Geometry & Topology
statement: Any set of (r-1)(d+1)+1 points in R^d can be split into r disjoint parts whose convex hulls have a common point.
short: Enough points guarantee a multiple intersection of hulls.
long: Enough points guarantee a multiple intersection of hulls. It generalizes Radon's theorem, the case r=2.
proof: Topological proofs use the Borsuk-Ulam theorem on a configuration space.
consequence: It is a central result of combinatorial geometry.

title: De Morgan's Laws for Sets and Logic
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: The complement of a union is the intersection of the complements, and the complement of an intersection is the union of the complements.
short: Negation swaps and/or.
long: Negation swaps and/or. The same laws hold for logical connectives and Boolean algebra.
proof: An element belongs to the left side exactly when it belongs to neither set, which is the right side.
consequence: They are fundamental for simplifying logical expressions.

title: Uniqueness of Binary Representation
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: Every positive integer has a unique representation as a sum of distinct powers of two.
short: Base-two expansion is unique.
long: Base-two expansion is unique. Repeated division by two produces the digits from least significant upward.
proof: Existence follows by repeated division; uniqueness follows from parity and induction on the quotient.
consequence: It underlies computer arithmetic and information theory.

title: Hamming Distance Is a Metric
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: The number of coordinates in which two equal-length strings differ satisfies the metric axioms.
short: Coordinate disagreements behave like distances.
long: Coordinate disagreements behave like distances. The triangle inequality holds coordinate by coordinate.
proof: Symmetry and identity of indiscernibles are immediate; if x and z differ at a coordinate then x,y or y,z differ there.
consequence: It is the natural distance for error-correcting codes.

title: Hamming Bound for Error-Correcting Codes
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: A q-ary code of length n and minimum distance d has size at most q^n divided by the volume of a Hamming ball of radius floor((d-1)/2).
short: Error balls around codewords must be disjoint.
long: Error balls around codewords must be disjoint. Codes meeting the bound are called perfect.
proof: Balls of radius t around distinct codewords cannot overlap, since otherwise their distance would be at most 2t.
consequence: It gives a fundamental limit on error correction.

title: Singleton Bound for Codes
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: A code of length n and minimum distance d has at most q to the power n-d+1 codewords.
short: Deleting d-1 coordinates separates all codewords.
long: Deleting d-1 coordinates separates all codewords. It is simple but often weaker than the Hamming bound.
proof: Puncture d-1 coordinates; if two codewords became equal their distance would be at most d-1.
consequence: It yields the notion of maximum distance separable codes.

title: Gilbert-Varshamov Bound
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: For every relative distance delta there exist binary codes with rate at least 1 minus the binary entropy of delta, up to lower-order terms.
short: Greedy coding ensures good codes exist.
long: Greedy coding ensures good codes exist. It is the best known general asymptotic existence bound for many parameters.
proof: Choose codewords greedily, excluding the union of Hamming balls around previously chosen words.
consequence: It guarantees codes with positive rate and positive relative distance.

title: Binary Hamming Codes Are Perfect
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: The binary Hamming code of length 2^m-1 has minimum distance three and meets the Hamming bound with equality.
short: Every word lies within one bit of exactly one codeword.
long: Every word lies within one bit of exactly one codeword. Its parity-check matrix lists all nonzero binary vectors of length m as columns.
proof: Syndromes identify all single-bit errors uniquely, so radius-one balls partition the space.
consequence: It gives an early and elegant example of perfect codes.

title: Binary Golay Codes
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: There is a perfect binary code of length 23, dimension 12 and minimum distance 7, whose extension to length 24 has minimum distance 8.
short: A rare perfect code with more than trivial parameters.
long: A rare perfect code with more than trivial parameters. The extended Golay code is deeply connected to the Leech lattice and sporadic groups.
proof: Construct the code via a generator matrix or quadratic residue construction and verify its minimum distance.
consequence: It is one of the most important exceptional codes.

title: Binary Reflected Gray Code
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: The reflected Gray code lists all n-bit words so that consecutive words differ in exactly one bit.
short: Flip one bit at a time to traverse all words.
long: Flip one bit at a time to traverse all words. The closed version also differs in one bit between the last and first word.
proof: Build the list recursively by prefixing 0 to the previous list and 1 to its reverse.
consequence: It reduces switching errors in analog-to-digital conversion.

title: Gale-Shapley Deferred Acceptance Algorithm
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: The deferred acceptance algorithm always produces a stable matching in the stable marriage problem.
short: Proposals and rejections converge to a stable pairing.
long: Proposals and rejections converge to a stable pairing. The version with men proposing gives the men-optimal stable matching.
proof: Once a woman rejects a man she never accepts him later, so the process terminates; a blocking pair would have proposed and been rejected.
consequence: It is used in school choice and residency matching.

title: Arrow's Impossibility Theorem
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: With at least three alternatives, no social welfare function satisfies unrestricted preferences, Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and non-dictatorship simultaneously.
short: Fair aggregation of rankings is impossible under these rules.
long: Fair aggregation of rankings is impossible under these rules. The theorem applies to ordinal rankings rather than cardinal utilities.
proof: Track decisive coalitions and show the family of decisive sets must be an ultrafilter, hence a dictatorship.
consequence: It reshaped social choice theory.

title: Condorcet Paradox
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: Individual transitive preferences can yield cyclical majority preferences.
short: Majority can be intransitive.
long: Majority can be intransitive. Three voters with cyclic orders produce the paradox.
proof: Give explicit rankings A>B>C, B>C>A, and C>A>B, then compare pairwise.
consequence: It motivates the study of voting rules beyond simple majority.

title: Gibbard-Satterthwaite Theorem
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: Every deterministic voting rule with at least three possible outcomes that is not a dictatorship is manipulable by some voter.
short: Strategy-proofness forces dictatorship.
long: Strategy-proofness forces dictatorship. It assumes voters have arbitrary preferences over outcomes.
proof: Reduce to Arrow's theorem via the interpretation of pivotal voters.
consequence: It is a central impossibility result in mechanism design.

title: Bertrand's Ballot Theorem
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: If candidate A receives p votes and candidate B receives q votes with p greater than q, the probability that A is strictly ahead throughout counting is (p-q)/(p+q).
short: The final margin determines the chance of never falling behind.
long: The final margin determines the chance of never falling behind. The result assumes a uniformly random ordering of the votes.
proof: Use the reflection principle on lattice paths from (0,0) to (p,q).
consequence: It is a classic application of path counting.

title: Primitive Roots Modulo a Prime
subject: Number Theory
statement: The multiplicative group of nonzero residues modulo a prime is cyclic, so a primitive root exists.
short: All nonzero residues are powers of one generator.
long: All nonzero residues are powers of one generator. There are phi(p-1) primitive roots modulo p.
proof: A finite subgroup of the multiplicative group of a field is cyclic.
consequence: It simplifies discrete logarithms and modular exponentiation.

title: Euler's Criterion for Quadratic Residues Modulo a Prime
subject: Number Theory
statement: For an odd prime p and integer a not divisible by p, a raised to (p-1)/2 is congruent to the Legendre symbol of a modulo p.
short: A power test decides quadratic residuosity.
long: A power test decides quadratic residuosity. The result is 1 for residues and -1 for nonresidues.
proof: Use Fermat's little theorem and the fact that the multiplicative group is cyclic.
consequence: It is the standard computational test for quadratic residues.

title: Counting Quadratic Residues Modulo a Prime
subject: Number Theory
statement: Among the nonzero residues modulo an odd prime p, exactly (p-1)/2 are quadratic residues and (p-1)/2 are nonresidues.
short: Squaring is two-to-one on nonzero classes.
long: Squaring is two-to-one on nonzero classes. The residues are the squares of 1 through (p-1)/2.
proof: The kernel of the squaring map on the cyclic group has size two.
consequence: It is the starting point for Legendre symbol properties.

title: Carmichael Numbers Fool Fermat's Test
subject: Number Theory
statement: Composite integers called Carmichael numbers can satisfy a^(n-1) congruent to 1 modulo n for every a coprime to n; the smallest is 561.
short: The converse of Fermat's little theorem is false.
long: The converse of Fermat's little theorem is false. Korselt's criterion characterizes them as squarefree composite n with p-1 dividing n-1 for every prime p dividing n.
proof: Check Korselt's criterion for 561: 2, 10, and 16 all divide 560.
consequence: They motivate stronger primality tests.

title: Infinitely Many Solutions to Pell's Equation
subject: Number Theory
statement: For any nonsquare positive integer D, the equation x squared minus D times y squared equals one has infinitely many integer solutions.
short: Units of a quadratic order generate infinitely many solutions.
long: Units of a quadratic order generate infinitely many solutions. The fundamental solution generates all positive solutions by powers.
proof: Continued fractions of sqrt(D) produce a nontrivial unit, whose powers give infinitely many.
consequence: It links Diophantine equations with algebraic number theory.

title: Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem for Irrationals
subject: Number Theory
statement: For any real alpha and positive integer N there are integers p and q with 1 <= q <= N and the distance from q alpha to an integer less than 1/N.
short: Pigeonhole gives good rational approximations.
long: Pigeonhole gives good rational approximations. It follows by considering fractional parts of multiples of alpha.
proof: Divide [0,1) into N intervals and find two multiples in the same interval, then take their difference.
consequence: It is the starting point of Diophantine approximation.

title: Minkowski's Convex Body Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: A centrally symmetric convex body in R^n with volume greater than 2^n times the determinant of a lattice must contain a nonzero lattice point.
short: Large symmetric bodies cannot avoid lattice points.
long: Large symmetric bodies cannot avoid lattice points. It is a foundational result of geometry of numbers.
proof: Apply Blichfeldt's theorem to the half-scaled body and compare translated copies.
consequence: It proves existence of solutions to many Diophantine inequalities.

title: LLL Lattice Basis Reduction
subject: Number Theory
statement: The LLL algorithm finds a reduced lattice basis in polynomial time whose first vector is within a fixed exponential factor of the shortest lattice vector.
short: Gram-Schmidt and size reduction yield short vectors.
long: Gram-Schmidt and size reduction yield short vectors. It works in dimension n with polynomial dependence on the bit size of the input.
proof: Maintain the Lovasz condition on Gram-Schmidt lengths and swap or size-reduce until it holds.
consequence: It is used in cryptography, Diophantine approximation, and integer programming.

title: Zeckendorf Representation
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: Every positive integer is uniquely a sum of nonconsecutive Fibonacci numbers.
short: Fibonacci numbers form a complete number system with no adjacent digits.
long: Fibonacci numbers form a complete number system with no adjacent digits. The greedy algorithm of subtracting the largest allowed Fibonacci number works.
proof: Existence follows by greedy choice; uniqueness follows because consecutive Fibonacci numbers are too close to substitute.
consequence: It gives Fibonacci coding and a curious alternative to binary.

title: Beatty's Partition Theorem
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: If r and s are positive irrational numbers with 1/r plus 1/s equal to one, the sequences of floors of nr and ns partition the positive integers.
short: Two complementary irrational slopes cover every integer once.
long: Two complementary irrational slopes cover every integer once. The golden ratio and its square give the classic example.
proof: Count terms up to N and show no integer can belong to both sequences, using the reciprocal condition.
consequence: It creates surprising partitions from irrational rotations.

title: Fibonacci Ratios Converge to the Golden Ratio
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: The ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers tends to the golden ratio, the positive root of x squared equals x plus one.
short: The recurrence settles into a fixed growth ratio.
long: The recurrence settles into a fixed growth ratio. Binet's closed form makes the limit immediate.
proof: Solve the characteristic equation of the Fibonacci recurrence and note the conjugate root has modulus below one.
consequence: It links recurrence sequences to continued fractions and aesthetics.

title: Sierpinski Triangle Dimension
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: The Sierpinski triangle is made of three scaled copies of itself by a factor one half, so its Hausdorff dimension is log 3 over log 2.
short: It is more than a curve but less than a region.
long: It is more than a curve but less than a region. Its area is zero while it has infinitely many boundary segments.
proof: Solve 3 times (1/2) to the dimension equals one for the self-similar pieces.
consequence: It is a canonical example of a fractal dimension.

title: Menger Sponge Has Zero Volume
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: Iteratively removing the middle sub-cubes from a cube yields a fractal with zero volume but unbounded surface area.
short: Removing 20 of 27 sub-cubes each step kills volume.
long: Removing 20 of 27 sub-cubes each step kills volume. At each step the remaining volume is multiplied by 20/27.
proof: Compute volume and area scaling factors geometrically after k iterations.
consequence: It illustrates pathological behavior of fractals.

title: Tower of Hanoi Minimum Moves
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: Moving n disks in the Tower of Hanoi requires exactly 2 to the n minus one moves.
short: Move the smaller stack twice and the largest disk once.
long: Move the smaller stack twice and the largest disk once. The standard recursive strategy is optimal.
proof: The largest disk must move once, requiring 2H_(n-1) moves of the smaller stack, giving the recurrence.
consequence: It is a classic example of exponential recursion.

title: Graham's Number
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: Graham's number is an enormous integer that arose as an upper bound for a Ramsey-theoretic question about colourings of hypercube edges.
short: Its size is beyond ordinary scientific notation.
long: Its size is beyond ordinary scientific notation. Later work gave much smaller bounds, but the number remains a famous illustration of rapid growth.
proof: It is defined by a finite recursion using Knuth's up-arrow notation.
consequence: It popularizes the scale of Ramsey-theoretic bounds.

title: Goodstein's Theorem
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: Every Goodstein sequence eventually reaches zero, although this cannot be proved in Peano arithmetic.
short: Organic-looking sequences terminate for ordinal reasons.
long: Organic-looking sequences terminate for ordinal reasons. The terms initially grow explosively before collapsing.
proof: Map each term to an ordinal below epsilon_0 that strictly decreases; Kirby and Paris showed unprovability in PA.
consequence: It is a concrete independence result for arithmetic.

title: Kruskal's Tree Theorem
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: Finite trees are well-quasi-ordered by homeomorphic embedding: every infinite sequence of trees has an earlier tree embedded in a later one.
short: Infinite tree sequences must contain an embedded pair.
long: Infinite tree sequences must contain an embedded pair. It is not provable in the predicative system ACA0.
proof: Nash-Williams proved the result; Friedman established its reverse-mathematical strength.
consequence: It appears in termination proofs and proof theory.

title: Busy Beaver Function Grows Too Fast to Compute
subject: Discrete Mathematics
