statement: The busy beaver function, giving the maximum steps or output of a halting Turing machine with n states, eventually exceeds every computable function.
short: Halting power encodes uncomputable growth.
long: Halting power encodes uncomputable growth. Its values are known only for very small state counts.
proof: If a computable upper bound existed, the halting problem could be decided by waiting past that bound.
consequence: It gives a concrete scale of uncomputability.

title: Kolmogorov Incompressibility Counting
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: For each n, most binary strings of length n have Kolmogorov complexity at least n, since there are fewer short descriptions than strings.
short: Most strings cannot be compressed.
long: Most strings cannot be compressed. Only 2^k strings can have descriptions of length k, so short descriptions are scarce.
proof: Count the number of programs of length less than n and compare with the number of n-bit strings.
consequence: It is the basis of algorithmic randomness.

title: Finite Fields Exist Exactly for Prime Power Orders
subject: Number Theory
statement: A finite field of order q exists if and only if q is a power of a prime, and it is unique up to isomorphism.
short: Prime powers are exactly the possible sizes.
long: Prime powers are exactly the possible sizes. The field is the splitting field of x^q-x over the prime subfield.
proof: Construct F_p^k as a quotient by an irreducible polynomial of degree k; conversely the characteristic prime divides q.
consequence: Finite fields underpin coding theory and cryptography.

title: Cantor Pairing Function
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: The expression (x+y)(x+y+1)/2 plus y gives an explicit bijection from pairs of natural numbers to natural numbers.
short: Enumerate pairs along successive diagonals.
long: Enumerate pairs along successive diagonals. It proves that the set of pairs of naturals is countable.
proof: Each diagonal x+y=s has s+1 entries and the formula lists diagonals in order.
consequence: It is a concrete encoding of pairs by single numbers.

title: Well-Ordering Theorem
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: Every set can be equipped with a well-order, meaning every nonempty subset has a least element.
short: The axiom of choice gives a least element to every subset.
long: The axiom of choice gives a least element to every subset. It is equivalent to the axiom of choice and to Zorn's lemma.
proof: Use a choice function to select elements recursively, or invoke Zorn's lemma on partial well-orderings.
consequence: It enables transfinite induction on arbitrary sets.

title: Power Set as a Boolean Algebra
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: The subsets of a set form a Boolean algebra under union, intersection, and complement, with empty set and the whole set as bounds.
short: Set operations obey the laws of Boolean algebra.
long: Set operations obey the laws of Boolean algebra. Union and intersection distribute over each other and every set has a complement.
proof: Verify the Boolean axioms elementwise.
consequence: It links logic, set theory, and circuit design.

title: Sperner's Lemma
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: If vertices of a triangulated simplex are labelled by simplex vertices so that boundary labels lie in the corresponding face, then there is a fully labelled small simplex, and the number of such simplices is odd.
short: Boundary conditions force a fully labelled cell.
long: Boundary conditions force a fully labelled cell. It is a combinatorial analogue of Brouwer's fixed-point theorem.
proof: Count label transitions along boundary edges and follow a path of adjacent fully labelled possibilities.
consequence: It gives constructive proofs of fixed-point theorems.

title: Hex Cannot End in a Draw
subject: Recreational Mathematics
statement: On a rhombus-shaped Hex board with opposite sides assigned to two players, a completely filled board always contains a connecting path for exactly one player.
short: A filled Hex board must have a winner.
long: A filled Hex board must have a winner. The result is equivalent to Brouwer's fixed-point theorem.
proof: A path of one colour separates the opposite sides, preventing the other player's connection; Sperner's lemma gives existence.
consequence: It explains why the game has no ties.

title: Konig's Infinity Lemma
subject: Discrete Mathematics
statement: Every infinite, locally finite, connected graph contains a ray: an infinite simple path starting at a given vertex.
short: Infinitely many finite branches force an infinite branch.
long: Infinitely many finite branches force an infinite branch. It is a standard compactness tool in graph theory and logic.
proof: Starting anywhere, infinitely many vertices lie in some finite-neighbour branch; choose one and iterate.
consequence: It proves the existence of infinite paths in infinite trees.
